units.la: Meteora orationis, ne quis nomine deceptus nescio quid magni expectet, nihil sunt aliud, quam dicta in speciem sublimia, revera inania atque vitiosa: quam appellationem à Longino Rhetore accepimus, qui ὑψηλά[?] in oratione & μετέωρα ita distinguit, ut illis vere sublimia, his vanam granditatis speciem præ se ferentia denotet. Quâ in re infelix, ut aliorum, vocabuli fatum fuit: nam cum ante idem quod ὑψηλὸν significaret, factum est abutentium culpa, ut in pejorem partem traheretur. Illi enim, qui scientiæ aut eloquentiæ sublimitatem ostentaturi, qua data occasione, de cœli meteoris loquebantur, μετέωρα sua identidem crepando, id tandem consecuti sunt, ut peculiari nomine μετεωρολέσχαι dici cœperint, qua voce, si Hesychio credimus, notantur οἱ τὰ ἄνω[?] ἐρανῶν μετέωρα φλυαροῦντες: unde & ipsa vox nescio quid odii contraxit, ut μετεωρολόγοι non modo dicerentur μεγαλορρήμονες atque inepti gloriosi, sed omnia in oratione vitiose [sublimia μετέωρα] à Rhetoribus appellarentur: prorsus, ut propter abusum nominis Phœbi evenit, ut omnes, qui altius in oratione, quam decet, se extollere volunt, Gallis hodiernis φοιβολογεῖν Phœbum loqui dicantur.
units.tr: The meteors of speech, lest anyone, taken in by the name, expect something great, are nothing other than sayings that seem sublime but are in fact empty and faulty. We have this designation from the rhetorician Longinus, who distinguishes the hypsēla [ὑψηλά] and the metewra [μετέωρα] in speech in such a way that he uses the former for things truly sublime and the latter for things that present a vain show of grandeur. In this matter the word had an unhappy fate, as others have had: for although it once meant the same as hypsēlon, it was dragged into a worse sense through the fault of those who misused it. Those who, wanting to display the lofty character of their learning or eloquence, spoke on occasion about the meteors of the heavens, and kept crowing their metewra [μετέωρα] again and again, at last brought it about that they began to be called by a special name, meteorolesxai [μετεωρολέσχαι], a word which, if we believe Hesychius, marks those who babble about the things above the heavens [οἱ τὰ ἄνω τῶν οὐρανῶν μετέωρα φλυαροῦντες]. Hence the word itself took on a certain hatred, so that the meteorologoi [μετεωρολόγοι] were called not only boastful and foolish braggarts, but every sublime thing in speech was called by the rhetoricians faultily [sublime metewra] [μετέωρα]. Just as, through the abuse of the name, it came about that all who wish to raise themselves higher in speech than is fitting are called by modern Frenchmen to phoibologein [φοιβολογεῖν], to speak Phoebus.

units.la: II. Quid in oratione μετέωρον sit, nequit intelligi, nisi prius, quid revera sit sublime, cognoscamus: id quod ante omnia planum est faciendum. Sine idem ὕψος[?] Longini & μέγεθος[?] Hermogenis, uti plerisque placuit, an hæc inter se differant, ut Tanaquillo Fabro visum fuit, atque elegantissimo Viro, cui Gallicam Longini versionem debemus: decidere nolumus. Confundant hæc, distinguant, quibus lubet: nobis dicendi præ[?]cepta tradere, non Rhetorum vocabula interpretari propofitum est.
units.tr: II. What is meteoron in speech cannot be understood unless we first know what is truly sublime, and this must be made clear before anything else. Whether this is the same as Longinus's hypsos [ὕψος] and Hermogenes' megethos [μέγεθος], as most have thought, or whether these differ from one another, as it seemed to Tanaquil Faber, and to that most elegant man to whom we owe the French version of Longinus, we are unwilling to settle. Let them confuse or distinguish these as they like: our purpose is to deliver the precepts of speaking, not to explain the terms of the rhetoricians.

units.la: III. Ad Grandem atque sublimem orationem, his enim vocibus idem significamus, primum omnium requiritur, ut res, de qua dicimus, grandis fit atque sublimis. Alia ab hominibus pluris, alia minoris aestimantur, quae pluris aestimantur majora, quae minoris, minora dicuntur: quae inter majora excellunt, ea magna, grandia & sublimia vocamus; producuntque haec in hominibus admirationem, quemadmodum ea, quae parva sunt, contemtus sequitur. Sunt igitur magna & sublimia ea omnia, quae, quod inter illa, quae homines aliis praeferre solent, excellunt, admiramur. Ita Reges magni sunt, quia eminent inter homines in dignitate constitutos, quos aliis anteponimus: Majores qui excellunt inter Reges: Maximus Rex Regum & Dominus dominantium: eademque ratione actiones & res magnae dicuntur. Magna vero sunt non tantum bona, sed etiam mala, quoniam & haec in suo genere excellentia admirationem pariunt: sic magna crudelitas dicitur, magnum flagitium, magna clades, magna miseria, magna jactura & id genus alia; quae bonis, quae in suo genere eminent, non modo non minora, sed majora vulgo habentur: eos enim in hominibus affectus excitant, qui objectum suum, ut loquuntur, mirum quantum augere & in majus extollere solent: ut sunt ira, indignatio, metus, tristitia, terror, desperatio: qui affectus tanto sunt in hominibus vehementiores iis, qui circa bonum versantur, quo major est fuga mali, quam appetitus boni. Hinc est, quod Reges valde superbi malint metui, quam diligi; quia parva etiam homines amare, sed non nisi magna metuere solent; amorque saepe contemtui vicinus est, nihil verò minus contemnimus, quam quod valde timemus. Malunt autem isti homines magni, quam boni videri; prorsus, ut boni appellatio multis nescio quam parvitatis significationem habere videatur. Hic vero non semper necesse est, ut res, de qua dicit Orator, sit magna judicio Philosophorum, qui in pretio rebus statuendo cum vulgo non conveniunt; sufficit, si talis est, aut communi hominum opinione, aut apud eos, apud quos dicimus, tum cum diximus, atque ibi, ubi dicimus. Sic Imperator, etsi divitias contemnat, cum milites spe prædæ ad prælium vult inflammare, potest de eâ magnificè loqui: de injuria etiam, tanquam de re magna dicere licet Oratori, quam fortasse Socrates aut Diogenes nihili faceret. Quin imò, si res per se magna, tanta Auditoribus non videtur, sublimi oratione non est utendum, nisi prius humiliori stylo, magisque rationum pondere, quam verborum magnificentia, id, de quo dicis, revera magnum esse probaveris: tum demum, si non vanis indiciis id te consecutum esse, animadvertis, assurgere potest oratio, atque elatior incedere. Hæcque causa est, quod pleraque orationis exordia modestiora esse conveniat: quia indecorum est tam magnificè loqui de argumento, quod, cum magnitudinem ejus nondum ostenderimus, potest auditori longè minus minus ac nobis videri.
units.tr: III. For a grand and sublime style (for we mean the same thing by these words), the first requirement is that the thing we are speaking about be grand and sublime. Some things are valued more highly by people, others less; those valued more highly are called greater, those valued less, lesser. Those things that excel among the greater ones we call great, grand and sublime, and these arouse admiration in people, just as what is small is followed by contempt. Therefore those things are great and sublime which, because they excel among those things that people usually prefer to others, we admire. Thus kings are great, because they stand out among men set in rank, whom we place above others; the greater are those who excel among kings; the Greatest King of Kings and Lord of Lords. By the same reasoning, actions and things are called great. Indeed, things are great not only when they are good but also when they are bad, since these too, being outstanding in their kind, cause admiration: thus we speak of great cruelty, a great disgrace, a great defeat, great misery, a great loss, and other things of that sort. Things that stand out in their kind as bad are commonly regarded not as lesser but as greater than the good: for they stir up in people those emotions which are wont to magnify their object, as they say, wonderfully and raise it to a greater size: such as anger, indignation, fear, sadness, terror, despair. These emotions are in people much more vehement than those that concern good things, in proportion as the flight from evil is stronger than the desire for good. Hence it is that very proud kings prefer to be feared rather than loved; because people are wont to love small things, but to fear only great ones; and love is often close to contempt, while we despise nothing less than what we greatly fear. Yet these great men prefer to seem great rather than good; so much so that the title of good seems to carry some sense of smallness. Here, however, it is not always necessary that the thing the orator speaks of be great in the judgement of the philosophers, who do not agree with the crowd in setting values on things; it is enough if it is such by common human opinion, or among those to whom we speak, at the time we speak, and in the place where we speak. Thus a general, though he despises riches, when he wants to fire his soldiers for battle with hope of plunder, may speak of them magnificently; and the orator may also speak of an injury as a great matter, though perhaps Socrates or Diogenes would think it of no account. Indeed, if a thing that is great in itself does not seem so great to the hearers, we must not use a sublime style, unless first, in a lower style and relying more on the weight of argument than on the splendour of words, you have shown that the matter you are speaking of really is great: then, and only then, if you notice that you have achieved this not by empty signs, can the speech rise and proceed in a more elevated manner. And this is the reason why most openings of speeches ought to be more modest: because it is unbecoming to speak so magnificently about a subject whose greatness we have not yet shown, and which may seem to the hearer far less great than it does to us.

units.la: IV. Neque verò ad dictionis sublimitatem sufficit, magnum orationis argumentum delegisse, ac nonnisi de rebus grandibus dicere velle: ingenium nostrum argumentum adæquet, necesse est; ut ejus, quod eximium est, magnam concipiamus in mente ideam, atque ita magnam, ut omnem ejus excellentiam cogitatione complectamur. Ingenium hic vocamus insignem imaginationis tum capacitatem, tum vim & vigorem. Capax imaginatio est, quæ simul aut saltem brevissimo tempore magnam rerum multitudinem, sine confusione, repræsentare potest; quæque propterea grande argumentum incredibili celeritate in omnes partes versat, omnia percurrit, quæ in eo maximè sunt admiranda, omnia cum quibus aut comparatum, aut quibus, oppositum majus videri possit. Vis imaginationis in eo consistit, ut ea omnia ac singula tam vividè menti nostræ repræsententur, ut non procul absit imaginatio à sensu, mensque non tam remota imaginari, quam præsentia cernere sibi videatur; quo fit, ut, quos aspectus harum rerum excitaret affectus, hos nuda in nobis excitet imaginatio. Hanc imaginationis & capacitatem & vim præcipuè in Poëtis admiramur: Capacitatem, cum imagines suas ex tot partibus componunt, tot in iis circumstantias exprimunt, ut concipi nequeat, quâ ratione hæc omnia in mentem illis venire potuerint. Vim & vigorem imaginationis miramur, cum hæc legentes, non tam legere, quam intueri nobis videmur, neque ab affectibus, quos præsens harum rerum conspectus concitare solet, temperare nobis possumus. Utrumque ad magnam in mente rei ideam atque imaginem formandam conjungi debet: qui priori carent, eorum oratio jejuna est ac sterilis, qui posteriori, illi elumbes ac languidi vocantur. Capacitas imaginationis in Ovidio nunquam desiderari poterit, nihil eo abundantius; vis interdum requiritur. Confer hujus Didonem cum Didone Virgiliana: dices, ibi Poetam loqui elegantissimum illum quidem, sed tamen Poetam: at hic Didonem ipsam plenam affectus, plenam desperationis.
units.tr: IV. Nor is it enough for sublimity of expression to have chosen a great subject for speech and to wish to speak only of grand things: it is necessary that our talent be equal to the subject, so that we conceive in our mind a great idea of what is outstanding, and great enough that we grasp all its excellence in thought. Here we call talent an outstanding both capacity and power and vigour of the imagination. An imagination has capacity when it can present at once, or at least in a very short time, a great multitude of things without confusion; and which therefore runs through a grand subject in all its parts with incredible speed, passing over everything in it that is most admirable, and everything with which it can be compared, or against which it may seem greater. The power of the imagination consists in this, that all these things, each and every one, are presented to our mind so vividly that the imagination is not far from sense, and the mind seems to see as present what it is not so much imagining as beholding; with the result that the imagination alone stirs up in us the same emotions that the sight of these things would arouse. We admire this capacity and power of imagination above all in the poets. We admire their capacity when they compose their images from so many parts and express in them so many circumstances that it cannot be conceived by what means all these things could have come into their minds. We admire the power and vigour of imagination when, as we read these things, we seem not so much to read them as to look upon them, and cannot restrain ourselves from the emotions which the present sight of such things is wont to stir. Both must be joined to form a great idea and image of a thing in the mind: those who lack the first have a dry and barren speech, and those who lack the second are called feeble and languid. The capacity of imagination can never be missed in Ovid; nothing is more abundant in him; but power is sometimes required. Compare his Dido with the Virgilian Dido: you will say that there the poet speaks, indeed most elegantly, yet still as a poet; but here Dido herself is full of emotion, full of despair.

units.la: V. At non omnes in dicendo imaginationis sunt partes, non præcipuæ; judicium ubique regnare debet,
units.tr: V. But in speaking, imagination does not hold the chief place in every part. Judgement must rule everywhere.

units.la: Scribendi recte sapere est & principium & fons.
units.tr: "To think soundly is both the beginning and the source of writing well."

units.la: Si in carmine non omnia statim effundenda sunt, quæ concitata & luxurians imaginatio suggerit, quanto major delectus est habendus in prosa oratione, cujus gravitas longè minus imaginationi indulget. Regat igitur judicium imaginationem, eique habenas modo relaxet, modo contrahat. Sit illud acre omnia pervidens, sit incorruptum, nihil dans propriorum conceptuum amori, sit severum & inexorabile, nihil indecens imaginationi condonans. Tale cum sit, discernat quid in illa, quam mente concipimus, imagine maximè sit admirandum: quid Auditores, hoc loco, hoc tempore maximè commoveat: Num generatim, quæ ad rei magnitudinem pertineat, proponere satis sit, an eundum sit per singulas partes, an gravissima tantum deligenda, an uni, quod inter cuncta eminet, sit insistendum idque vividissimis coloribus exprimendum: an etiam tegendum sit, quod maximæ admirationi esse volumus, sed ita tegendum, ut nescio quid magni tegi videatur. Fingat imaginem suam, refingat imaginatio, donec judicio placeat. Vertatur in omnes partes, donec severus iste judex pronunciet: hæc parte maximè est admirabilis, hæc auditoribus obvertenda.
units.tr: If in poetry not everything that an excited and luxuriant imagination suggests should be poured out at once, how much greater selection must be made in prose, whose gravity indulges imagination far less. Let judgement therefore govern the imagination, loosening its reins now and tightening them now. Let it be sharp, seeing through everything; let it be incorruptible, granting nothing to love of its own conceptions; let it be strict and unyielding, pardoning nothing unseemly in the imagination. Being such, let it decide what in the image we conceive in our mind is most admirable, and what most moves the hearers here and now. Is it enough to set forth in general terms what pertains to the greatness of the matter, or must one go through the individual parts, or choose only the weightiest, or dwell on the one thing that stands out above the rest and express it in the most vivid colours? Or should what we wish to be greatly admired be concealed, but concealed in such a way that something great seems to be hidden? Let the imagination shape its image and reshape it until it pleases judgement. Let it be turned on every side until that stern judge pronounces: this part is most admirable; this is what must be presented to the hearers.

units.la: VI. Postquum absoluta est in mente rei magnæ imago atque à judicio probata: de verbis, quibus, tanquam coloribus, eam aliis depingamus, soliciti esse debemus, ut quanta nobis, tanta & illis videatur. Verba igitur imaginem aquare debent, ut imago rem: unde & hæc in grandi oratione grandia & sublimia esse oportet. Fit autem hoc tribus modis: auctoritate utentium, sono, & significatione. Auctoritate utentium sublimia sunt verba, quæ non ex hara, ex ergastulis, atque ex triviis petuntur, lixis & calonibus in deliciis sunt, sed hominum liberaliter educatorum, nobilium, atque in eminentia constitutorum communi usu trita. Qualia verba in omnibus linguis politiores atque elegantiores ab ijs, quæ sordidorum hominum usu viluerunt, facile distinguunt. Verba cum dico, phrases etiam, quas vocant, proverbia, & quæ sunt his similia, intelligo. Sono grandia sunt verba, incisa, membra, periodi, hæc enim omnia ad verborum sonum pertinent, si majorem sonum edunt, si aures implent, percellunt, & tantum non terrent aliquando, ut cum apud Virgilium venti ex cavernis erumpunt, aut cum crines effusa sacerdos Tercentum tonat ore Deos, Erebumque Chaosque Tergeminamque Hecatem. aut cum apud Claudianum Ceres, amissa filia, toto bacchatur Olympo, Sed hæc auribus dijudicantur, quas alij alijs elegantiores habent. Maxima vero verborum sublimitas in significatione consistit; ubi nemo est, qui nescit, aliud vocabulum plus alio significare: ita amare plus significare, quam diligere, flagitare, quam petere, erumpere, quam evadere. Ad orationis igitur granditatem non tantum facit, vocabulis uti, quæ res magnas significant, sed ea deligere, quæ plus significant. Ita grandius est illud: furor arma ministrat, quam si iram Poëta dixisset. Sunt autem præter notiores & præcipuas cujuslibet vocis significationes innumerabiles aliæ, quas cum illis usus hominum conjunxit, secundarias quidam vocant: ita si quem furem appellas, non id tantum dicis, abstulisse hunc hominem aliquid invito Domino, quæ præcipua vocis est significatio: alia plura simul innuis: te illi homini iratum esse, verbo hoc te vindictam quærere, te illum de industria offendere velle, & usq; eò contemnere, ut iram illius provocando ultionem non metuas: significas etiam aliquando hoc verbo; te hominem esse parum politum. Pauca sunt verba, quae non complures hujus generis significationes adjunctas habent; quae cum in omni orationis genere, tum in sublimi potissimum sunt observandae, non modo, ut nihil significemus voce, quod significare nolumus, sed ut his quoque verborum significationibus orationis sublimitatem augeamus. Quantum Caesar dixit, cum unica voce, Quirites, seditiosum exercitum compescuit? frustra in Lexicis quaeres omnes hujus verbi significationes, quas milites tumultuantes, illo audito, intellexerunt. Imo dicere posfumus, nulla re orationem grandiorem fieri, quam vocibus, quae multas hujus generis significationes habent. Sic enim fit, ut in paucis verbis iisque simplicissimis grandis lateat sensus, quo nihil est in oratione sublimius. Ita Valerius Poplicola vindex Romanae libertatis, qui Romanis in regni affectati suspicionem venit, ob aedes in monte Velia exstructas: Non obstabunt, inquit, Publii Valerii aedes libertati vestrae, Quirites, tuta vobis erit Velia. Deferam non in planum modo aedes, sed colli etiam subjiciam, ut vos supra suspectum me civem habitetis. In Velia aedificent quibus melius, quam P. Valerio creditur libertas. Nihil sublimius legi potest; at ut videas, quam pauca verba quantum significare possint, dele repetitum P. Valerii nomen, & illa verba, suspectum civem: videbis quantum de sublimitate eorum detraxeris. Jam illa Ciceronis: Consul videt, hic tamen vivit, quam sublimia sunt? quantum significant hic verba, Senatus, consulis a Cicerone Consule in Senatu dicta? quanto minus dixisset, si dixisset: Vos hoc intelligitis & ego video? Eum in finem inventae sunt figurae, ut praeter rem affectus nostros declararent; Ita in eadem oratione, cum Cicero exclamat: O tempora, o mores, non simpliciter morum temporumque perversitatem notat; sed simul exprimit, quanto se dolore haec morum temporumque depravatio afficiat. Alios affectus aliae figurae produnt. Tropis etiam grandisfit oratio, metaphoris praecipue, sed in loco adhibitis: nunquam autem iis locus est in sublimi oratione, nisi sint necessarii, aut ad orationis varietatem, aut cum propria verba rei magnitudinem non satis exprimere videntur: tum vero recurrimus imus ad voces, quæ res majores significant, easque cum propriis permutamus. Sed in troporum doctrinâ Rhetores multi sunt, imo nimii.
units.tr: VI. Once the image of a great matter has been completed in the mind and approved by judgement, we ought to be anxious about the words with which we paint it for others, as with colours, so that it may appear to them as great as it appears to us. Words therefore ought to match the image as the image matches the thing. Hence in grand discourse the words too must be grand and lofty. This comes about in three ways: by the authority of those who use them, by sound, and by meaning. Words are lofty by the authority of those who use them when they are not taken from the field, the workhouse or the crossroads, nor are favourites of camp-followers and hucksters, but are worn by the common usage of people who are liberally educated, noble and placed in high station. Such words, in every language, easily distinguish the more refined and elegant from those that have grown cheap through the use of base men. By words I mean also what are called phrases, proverbs and things like them. Words are grand by sound when clauses, members and periods, for all of these belong to the sound of words, produce a fuller sound, fill the ears, strike, and sometimes almost terrify. Thus in Virgil the winds burst from their caves, and the priestess with hair flowing thunders with her mouth three hundred gods, Erebus and Chaos and triple-bodied Hecate. Thus in Claudian Ceres, having lost her daughter, rages through all Olympus. But such things are judged by the ear, and different men find different things more elegant. The greatest loftiness of words, however, lies in meaning, where everyone knows that one word signifies more than another: to love signifies more than to esteem, to demand more than to seek, to burst out more than to escape. Thus to the grandeur of speech it contributes not only to use words that signify great things, but to choose those that signify more. So "fury supplies arms" is grander than if the poet had said "anger." Besides the better-known and chief meanings of any word there are countless others, which common usage has joined to them, and which some call secondary. So if you call someone a thief, you say not only the chief meaning of the word, that this man has taken something from its unwilling owner; you also imply many other things at once: that you are angry with that man, that by this word you seek vengeance, that you wish to offend him deliberately, and that you despise him so far that you do not fear his anger provoked into punishment. Sometimes too by this word you signify that the man is ill-bred. Few are the words that do not have several such meanings attached; these must be observed in every kind of speech, but especially in the lofty, not only so that we say nothing by a word that we do not wish to signify, but so that we also increase the loftiness of speech by these secondary meanings of words. How much did Caesar say when with the single word Quirites he quelled a mutinous army! In vain would you seek in the lexicons all the meanings of this word which the rioting soldiers understood when they heard it. Indeed we may say that nothing makes speech grander than words that have many meanings of this kind. For in this way a great sense lies hidden in a few words, and these very simple, and nothing in speech is more sublime. So Valerius Poplicola, champion of Roman liberty, who fell under suspicion of aiming at kingship because of the house he had built on the Velia hill, said: "Publius Valerius's house will not stand in the way of your liberty, Quirites; the Velia will be safe for you. I will lower the house not only onto the level ground but I will place it beneath the hill, so that you may live above a citizen whom you suspect." Let those build on the Velia to whom liberty is trusted better than to Publius Valerius. Nothing more sublime can be read. But to see how much a few words can signify, delete the repeated name Publius Valerius and the words a suspected citizen; you will see how much of their loftiness you have taken away. Then that saying of Cicero's: "The consul sees, yet this man lives", how sublime it is! How much do the words Senate and consul, spoken by Cicero the consul in the Senate, signify! How much less he would have said if he had said: "You understand this, and I see it." To this end figures were invented, so that beyond the matter they might declare our feelings. Thus in the same speech, when Cicero cries out: "O the times, O the morals!", he does not merely note the perversity of morals and times; at the same time he expresses how deeply this depravity of morals and times affects him. Other figures reveal other feelings. Speech also becomes grand through tropes, especially metaphors, but when they are used in their proper place. Yet in lofty speech they have no place unless they are necessary*, either for variety of style, or when proper words seem not to express the greatness of the matter sufficiently. Then indeed we have recourse to words that signify greater things and exchange them for the proper ones. But in the teaching on tropes the rhetoricians are many, indeed too many.

units.la: VII. Quæ hactenus dicta sunt, sufficere plerisque videbuntur ad dictionis sublimitatem; sed unum mihi restare videtur, quod haud scio an sit præcipuum. Orator non argumentum modo suum oratione depingit, sed se ipsum, πάντος λόγῳ ἰδεῖν τὸ ἦθος τῷ χαρακτῆρι[?], verissime Demetrius μνημεῖαι[?] ait. Videndum igitur in sub-limem genere, ut non rem modo sub-limem pingamus, sed animum. Animum dico, non ingenium, quod in animo humili & pusillo interdum magnum est. Est autem magnus animus atque excelsus ejus, qui omni affectu ita in res magnas atque eximias fertur, ut his unice delectetur, his lubentissime occupetur, atque adeo totum se his tradat, ut ea, quæ viles animæ maximi faciunt, tanquam ad se non magnopere pertinentia, despiciat; in omni fortunâ sibi constans, semper liber, semper sui juris, verus, simplex, apertus, recti tenax; conservans ita dignitatem suam, ut propter nullius rei aut spem aut metum, aut aliam quampiam perturbationem, ad ea, quæ se indigna judicat, demittatur, atque abjiciatur. Talem se pingat Orator, si majestatem orationi quandam vult conciliare. Talem se pingit integro orationis habitu, qui non putidam diligentiam, & Rhetorum scholas redolet, angusti enim animi hæc sunt, sed in quâ elucet eloquentia mascula, simplex, candida; quæ in illis est, qui dicunt, quod sentiunt; qui magis curant, quid dicant, quam quomodo; qui denique bene dicunt, non quod volunt benedicere, sed quod aliter dicere non possunt. Talem se declarat nobili quadam dicendi libertate & [?]παῤῥησία[?], quam ubique spirat oratio, quæ, ut nihil agreste & rusticum habet, ita aliena est à puerili pudore, servili timore, atque turpi adulatione. Affectus ipsi, qui in plerisque hominibus impotentis animi signa sunt, in tanto Oratore generosi videntur, quales sunt ira Neptuni apud Virgilium: lacrymæ Ciceronis in oratione pro Milone. Sparsis denique per orationem sententiis animi magnitudinem prodit Orator, ita tamen, ut hæ orationi non de industriâ afsutæ, sed ut sibi nonnisi de argumento cogitanti, ideo quod res ita ferebat, excidisse videantur. Haec animi magnitudo declarari vix potest, ubi non est: si illam simulare velis, oftentatio ipsa & affectatio, aut metaphora interdum a re levi petita, aut figura grandis in humiliori argumento te proder. In hac animi magnitudine exprimenda regnat Livius, cum ubique, tum in concionibus. Has cum legis, non Livium te legere, sed ipsos illos rerum Dominos te audire tibi videris. Huc pertinent quaedam priscorum apophthegmata. Nolo furari viAlexander dixit; si divinandum foret, cujus hoc esset dictum, Alexandri dicerent, qui Alexandrum noffent. Et quis, nisi Alexander, Parmenioni dicenti, Facerem hoc, si Alexander essem, ita respondisset, & ego, si essem Parmenio. Illud Cafarem vehis, quantam rem significat, sed quantum etiam animum? Circumfertur hodie dictum Ducis Genuensis, qui in Galliam ire coactus, ut Reipublicae nomine Regi Galliarum se submitteret, postquam illi, quicquid Lutetiae splendoris habet, monstratum esset, interrogatus, quid in urbe & aula toto orbe celeberrima maxime vidisset admirandum: haud cunctatus, Me, inquit. Cui responso nihil prorsus deest ad sublimitatem. Maxima res dicitur, unica simplici sed significantissima voce dicitur, summamque excelsi animi significationem habet.
units.tr: VII. What has been said so far will seem sufficient to most people for the loftiness of style; but one thing still seems to me to remain, and I am not sure whether it is not the chief one. The orator paints not only his subject in his speech but himself; Demetrius most truly says that in every speech the character [πάντος λόγῳ ἰδεῖν τὸ ἦθος τῷ χαρακτῆρι] is seen [μνημεῖαι]. In the lofty style, therefore, we must take care to paint not only the sublime matter but the spirit. I say spirit, not talent, which in a humble and petty spirit is sometimes great. A great and lofty spirit is that of the man who, in every feeling, is carried towards great and distinguished things in such a way that he delights in these alone, is most willingly occupied with these, and so gives himself wholly to them that he looks down on what base minds hold in highest esteem, as things that do not much concern him. In every fortune he is constant to himself, always free, always his own master, true, simple, open, and tenacious of what is right. He keeps his dignity so that, on account of no hope or fear of anything, or any other disturbance, he is never lowered or cast down to those things that he judges unworthy of himself. Such a man the orator must depict himself as, if he wishes to lend a certain majesty to his speech. Such a man is revealed in a whole habit of speech, which does not smell of a foul fussiness or of the schools of the rhetoricians, for these belong to narrow spirits, but in which shines a manly, simple and candid eloquence, such as belongs to those who say what they feel, who care more about what they say than how they say it, and who in short speak well not because they wish to speak well but because they cannot speak otherwise. Such a man reveals himself by a certain noble freedom of speech [παῤῥησία], which breathes through every part of the speech; and as it has nothing rustic or boorish, so it is far from childish shame, servile fear and base flattery. The feelings themselves, which in most men are signs of an unrestrained spirit, appear noble in so great an orator, as Neptune's anger does in Virgil, or Cicero's tears in the speech for Milo. Finally, by maxims scattered through the speech the orator reveals the greatness of his spirit, yet in such a way that these do not seem to have been contrived deliberately to adorn the speech, but to have slipped out of a man who was thinking only of his subject, because the matter itself brought them forth. This greatness of spirit can scarcely be displayed where it does not exist; if you wish to feign it, the very ostentation and affectation will betray you, whether by a metaphor sometimes taken from a trivial matter, or by a grand figure used in a lowly subject. In expressing this greatness of spirit Livy reigns supreme, everywhere, and especially in his speeches. When you read these you seem not to be reading Livy, but to be hearing the very masters of affairs themselves. To this belong certain sayings of the ancients: "I do not wish to steal the victory," said Alexander; if one had to guess whose saying this was, those who knew Alexander would say it was Alexander's. And who but Alexander, when Parmenio said, "I would do this if I were Alexander," would have answered, "And I, if I were Parmenio." Consider how much that saying of Caesar's signifies, and how much spirit it reveals too. Today there is a saying going round of the Duke of Genoa, who, having been compelled to go to France to submit himself to the King of France on behalf of the Republic, was shown everything splendid that Paris contains, and when asked what he had found most admirable in the city and court, the most famous in the whole world, answered without hesitation: "Me." Nothing at all is lacking in this reply for sublimity. A great matter is spoken of, spoken in a single simple but most significant word, and it has the highest expression of a lofty spirit. Of this sublimity there is an incredible power: those who read or hear such sayings feel, while reading and hearing, their own spirit also raised by the speech and conceiving noble impulses. Even when the truth is unwelcome, in which this sublimity appears, men take delight; and ...

units.la: Hujus sublimitatis incredibilis quaedam vis est: ut iltius[?]modi dicta qui legunt, qui audiunt, inter legendum & audiendum sentiant, cum oratione suum quoque animum attolli, & generosos impetus concipere. Etiam inimica veritate, in qua haec sublimitas apparet, homines delectantur: & quae alias odium parerent, tunc admirationem excitat. Alexander piratae vitam condonasse dicitur, his verbis causam dicenti: Ego quoniam unico navigiolo maria infesto, pirata nominor, tu, quum idem facias magna classe, Rex appellaris. Noluit nimirum Rex animi magnitudine, quam dictum hoc declarat, piratae cedere.
units.tr: There is an incredible power in this sublimity: when people read or hear such sayings, they feel, while reading and hearing, their own spirit lifted up by the speech and conceiving noble impulses. People even take delight in the truth that is hostile to them, in which this sublimity appears, and what would otherwise stir up hatred now stirs up admiration. Alexander is said to have pardoned the life of a pirate, who pleaded his case with these words: Since I am called a pirate because I harass the seas with a single little boat, you, because you do the same with a great fleet, are called a king. Clearly the king, by this saying, declared his greatness of spirit, and he would not yield to the pirate.

units.la: VIII. Ex his, quae dicta sunt, cuique nunc manifestum est, quantum hoc sit, non unum atque alterum sublime dictum, sed sublimis oratio. In hac qui excellere cupit, hoc, ut paucis verbis, quae adhuc dixi, comprehendam, requiritur, ut magnam quandam rei grandis ideam, simulque animi sui sublimitatem verbis verbis tam significantibus exprimat, ut auditores & in argumenti, & in animi sui admirationem rapiat. Hujus rei difficultas, si quos ab hoc dicendi genere absterret, sapiunt illi mea quidem fententia, possunt enim in alio genere non modo placere sed eminere. Paucissimi in sublimi dictione tolerabiles sunt, excellit fortasse unus & alter, si modo excellunt. Reliqui omnes, quo magis se attollere volunt, eo magis aut judicij, aut ingenii aut animi humilitatem produnt, dumque humum vitant, nubes & inania captant, dum sublimia sectantur, in μετεώρα incidunt, ut omnis μετεώρων origo à male affectatâ orationis sublimitate proveniat. Sed de his nunc, ut plura dicamus, instituti ratio requirit.
units.tr: VIII. From what has been said, it is now plain to everyone how much depends not on one or another sublime saying, but on a sublime style. Whoever wishes to excel in it needs, to sum up in a few words what I have said so far, to express in words so expressive a great idea of a great matter, and at the same time the loftiness of his own spirit, that the hearers are swept away both into admiration of the subject and into admiration of his spirit. If the difficulty of this kind of writing deters some, I think they are wise, for they can not only please but excel in another kind. Very few are tolerable in the sublime style, and perhaps one or two excel, if indeed they do excel. All the rest, the more they try to raise themselves, the more they betray a lack of judgement, wit or spirit. While they avoid the ground, they grasp at clouds and emptiness; while they pursue the lofty, they fall into the meteora [μετεώρα]. So every meteor of speech arises from a badly affected sublimity of style. But to say more about these matters, the plan of this work requires that I now turn to them.

units.la: IX. Omnia orationis meteora ad tria genera referri possunt, aut enim oratio verè sublimis rei humili accommodatur, aut non vera est in argumento magno granditas orationis: aut denique neque res sublimis est, neque vera dictionis sublimitas. Primum genus duas cauflas habet: vel enim majoris facimus res leves atque revera sunt, & hinc illi clamores; vel existimamus, apte & elegantèr de nulla re dici posse, nisi magnifice dicatur. Prius animi humilitatem, utrumque judicii infirmitate arguit. Dici non potest, quot sint hujus vitii exempla. Plerunque literati, cum de rebus suis loquuntur, nimis magnificâ oratione utuntur, fortasse, quia nimis magnificè de rebus suis sentiunt. Omnes dicendi figuras, quae vehementissimos affectus significant, impendunt, ut dicant, quomodo hoc aut illud sit legendum, quid haec aut illa vox significet, quâ methodo ars aliqua sit tradenda, &c. Julius Cæsar Scaliger, magnum inter literatos nomen, Sylvio Filio, postquam is prima latinae linguae rudimenta didicerat, accuratiorem hujus linguae rationem traditurus, ita de hac re loquitur. Egressum te ex angustiis tenuioris literaturæ, Sylvi Cæsar fili, non ante decet inire rationem graviorum studiorum, quam istarum praeceptionum caussas notas habeas, per quas excellentissimæ cujusque scientiæ cursus aperiri debuit. Quanquam enim haec ipsa tenes, quæ certis observationibus recepta sunt, tamen quia sapius dubitare, an ita sit, semper quaerere, quae sint talia, cogi possis, nisi te exemtum ex his difficultatibus in tuto collocatum videam, vitam mihi acerbam putem. Et paulo post: Ætati quidem tua, Fili mi, quanquam primo in congressu videantur hæc asperiuscula: ita tamen velim cum animo tuo statuas, Nihil unquam vulgare precium ullum opera fecisse. At quanti tandem sit, excellentissimis quibusque rebus a vita ipsius primordiis assuescere? Itaque tetrica hæc nonnisi barbaris[?] atque incultis animis terrorem, ac desperationis[?] facere opinionem, pro nobis vero appetentibus veritatis tanquam armatas stare putes legiones. Diceres Hamilcarem Hannibalem filium ad bellum perpetuum Romanis faciendum inflammare: aut saltem Julium Cæsarem nostrum Sylvium suum, quâ virtute amissum Veronæ principatum recuperare possit, docere; non filio patrem præcepta Grammatica tradere. Huc pertinet Ludovici Vivis de Christ. Longolio judicium, Verba illum, ait, habere Ciceroniana, at sensu ineptiorem esse, propterea, quod dicta grandia rebus exiguis aptarit. Non enim, inquit, satis illi erat, verba & phrasin Ciceronis miro studio imitari, nisi etiam totum Ciceronem exprimeret, rem illam publicam simularet & curam imperii, quo totus continebatur orbis. Privatus ipse & in angulum studiosi secessus abditus, in quo tam erat ridiculus, quam si gigantis vestitum induisset, & verba ac pronunciationem gigantis effingeret, ut gigas videretur. Nunquam magis hoc meteori genus apparet, quam in ejus Apologia, in quâ ita adversus frivolas quasdam otiosorum hominum accusationes se defendit, ut Rex Angliæ Carolus I. hoc seculo capitis caussam dicere coactus, majori verborum magnificentiâ uti non potuisset. Hæc pluribus facete, ut solet, prosequitur Erasmus. In idem vitium incidunt non reliqui modo Ciceroniani, sed plerique imitatores. Imitantur maximorum Virorum dictionem, qui? Umbratici homines, in museo latentes, nonnisi pueris, adolescentibus, aut quibusdam sui similibus noti. Imitantur loquentes de rebus gravissimis, atque adeo admirandis, qui? qui nihil, quod dicant, habent, si ea exceperis, quæ ad studia literarum pertinent. T. Livii imitator, quoties in loci alicujus lectione, aut sententia hæret, non aliter loquitur, ac si Romanus exercitus in furcis Caudinis hæreret. Si quis in docendi methodo aliquid innovat, Salustii amator ab hoc scriptore colores ad hominis audaciam depingendam mutuabitur, quibus ille Catilinam depinxit. Cui Tacitus in delitiis est, is cum de disciplina Scholastica, aut de artibus tradendis agitur, sententias loquetur,obscura oracula fundet: diceres,eum occultas Regnantium artes & arcana dominationis aperire. Frequens Q.Curtii lector de lucubratiunculis eruditorum non aliter loquetur,atque Alexander de Asia subjugata. Hic imagines Velleji Paterculi, quibus tot Heroas expressit, cuilibet amicorum, quem laudare vult,accommodat. Ille Bella Grammaticalia & doctorum rixas describit ea pompa,qua Florus bella Populi Romani. Quid quæris? Nulla urbs est tam obscura, nullum oppidum tam parvum, in quo non Romanorum scriptorum imitatores forum,comitium,rostra,Capitolium,sellas curules,fasces,securos,trabeas,ovationes,triumphos, omnem deniq;,tanquam in compendio,inveniant antiquę urbis majestatem. Qui quidem omnes recte fortasse cum Tityro Virgiliano dicerent:
units.tr: IX. All the meteors of speech can be referred to three kinds. For either a truly sublime style is applied to a humble matter, or there is no truth in the grandeur of style for a great subject; or finally the matter is neither sublime nor is the style truly lofty. The first kind has two causes: either we make trivial matters greater than they really are, and hence those shouts; or we think that a matter cannot be aptly and elegantly described unless it is described magnificently. The former reveals a humble spirit, the latter a weakness of judgement. It cannot be said how many examples of this fault there are. Very often scholars, when they speak of their own affairs, use a rather grand style, perhaps because they think too grandly of their own affairs. They bring in all the figures of speech that signify the most vehement passions, to tell us how this or that is to be read, what this or that word means, by what method some art is to be taught, and so on. Julius Caesar Scaliger, a great name among scholars, when his son Sylvius had learned the first rudiments of the Latin tongue and he was about to deliver a more exact account of this language, speaks on this matter as follows: Son Sylvius Caesar, having come out of the narrow confines of the lesser learning, it is not fitting for you to enter upon the plan of the weightier studies before you know the reasons for those precepts, through which the course of every most excellent science ought to be opened. For although you hold these very things that have been received by certain observations, nevertheless, because you are often able to be forced to doubt whether it is so, and always to ask what such things are, unless I see you freed from these difficulties and placed in safety, I should think my life bitter. And a little later: For your age, my son, although at first meeting these things may seem rather harsh, nevertheless I should like you to resolve in your mind that nothing ever achieved any value without effort. But how much, after all, does it matter to grow accustomed to the most excellent things from the very beginnings of life? And so these stern precepts, you may think, create terror and an opinion of despair only in barbarous and uncultivated minds, but for us who long for truth they stand like armed legions. You would say that Hamilcar was inflaming his son Hannibal to wage perpetual war on the Romans, or at least that our Julius Caesar was teaching his Sylvius by what virtue he could recover the principate lost at Verona; not that a father was handing down the precepts of grammar to his son. To this belongs the judgement of Lodovicus Vives on Christian Longolius: he says that he has Ciceronian words, but is more foolish in sense, because he has fitted grand expressions to trivial matters. For, he says, it was not enough for him to imitate with wonderful zeal the words and phrasing of Cicero, unless he also expressed the whole Cicero, feigning that public affairs and the cares of empire, by which the whole world was held. He was a private man, hidden away in a corner of studious retirement, in which he was as ridiculous as if he had put on the dress of a giant and affected the words and pronunciation of a giant, so that he might seem a giant. This kind of meteor never appears more clearly than in his Apology, in which he defends himself against certain trivial accusations of idle men in such a way that King Charles I of England, forced in this century to plead for his head, could not have used greater pomp of words. Erasmus pursues these matters at more length, wittily, as is his way. Into the same fault fall not only the Ciceronians but most of the imitators. They imitate the style of the greatest men; who are they? Shadowy figures, hidden in a museum, known only to boys, young men, or a few like themselves. They imitate those who speak of the gravest and even most admirable matters; and who are they? Men who have nothing to say, if you except those things that pertain to literary studies. The imitator of T. Livy, whenever he sticks at the reading of some passage or at a sentence, speaks no differently than if the Roman army were stuck in the Caudine Forks. If someone introduces some innovation in the method of teaching, the lover of Sallust will borrow from that writer the colours with which to depict the man's audacity, the colours with which he depicted Catiline. He to whom Tacitus is a delight, when the discipline of the school or the teaching of the arts is under discussion, will utter maxims and pour forth obscure oracles: you would say that he was revealing the hidden arts of rulers and the secrets of domination. The frequent reader of Quintus Curtius will speak of the little lucubrations of scholars no differently than Alexander spoke of the subjugation of Asia. Here the images of Velleius Paterculus, with which he portrayed so many heroes, he applies to any friend he wishes to praise. Another describes the grammatical wars and the quarrels of the learned with the pomp with which Florus describes the wars of the Roman people. What more? There is no city so obscure, no town so small, in which the imitators of Roman writers do not find, as if in an epitome, the forum, the assembly, the rostra, the Capitol, curule chairs, fasces, axes, togas, ovations, triumphs, and in short all the majesty of the ancient city. Who all, perhaps, might rightly say with Virgil's Tityrus:

units.la: Urbem quam dicunt Romam Melibae putavi / Stultus ego huic nostra similem.
units.tr: I thought the city they call Rome was like our own, Meliboeus, a fool that I was.

units.la: Magis ridiculi quam ille,qui exiguum fluviolum ita descri-psit: ὃς ἀπὸ τῶν Ταυ[?]ῶν ὀρέων ὁρμώμενον ἐκ[?]ίεσθαι εἰς θάλασσαν: tan- quam si de Nili aut Euphratis impetu fuislet dicendum. Imo, quod mireris, nostri Romani magistratus Romanos togatos pariter & sagatos non in civili modo cujuslibet urbis republica in-veniunt,sed in republica etiā,uti loquuntur,literaria. Huicq; adeo Reipublicæ Michaël Fernus Poemata Campani his verbis dedicat: Dictatori Perpetuo, Imperatori nostro Maximo, Pomponio Lęto, Magistro equitum, cunctaque Respublica literaria, Michael Fernus Mediolanensis vilis pabulator strenuam pugnam, pulchram victoriam. Huc pertinent ii, quibus semper in ore sunt magna Vetustatis nomina: Magnum illum Alexandrum aiunt: Pyrrhum Epirotarum Regem praedicant; Quod Furio quondam Camillo accidit: Hannibal ille terror Roma: Quintus Fabius, M. Marcellus, ille scutum,hic gladius P.R. Imperitus historiæ,tanta nomina toties audiens in Academicis orationibus,merito quæreret,num hi omnesDoctores fuerint,aut L.A.Magistri.Quædam horum nominum nimio usu in Gallia usque eò viluerunt, ut nisi quis explodi velit,in oratione Cambysen aut Epiminondam appellare non audeat; si quando de his necessario loquendum est, circuitione uti oportet. Hunc magnorum nominum in re exigua abusum facete ridet Martialis epigrammate in Postumum.
units.tr: More ridiculous still was the man who described a small stream thus: which, rising from the Taurus mountains and discharging into the sea [ὃς ἀπὸ τῶν Ταυ[?]ῶν ὀρέων ὁρμώμενον ἐκ[?]ίεσθαι εἰς θάλασσαν], as if he had to speak of the rush of the Nile or the Euphrates. Indeed, what is remarkable, our Romans find Roman magistrates in the civil government of any city whatever, togated and sagated alike, and not only in the civil government but also, as they put it, in the literary republic. To this very republic Michael Fernus dedicates his Poems of Campanus in these words: To the Perpetual Dictator, our Greatest Emperor, Pomponius Laetus, Master of the Horse, and the whole literary republic, Michael Fernus of Milan, a humble provider, sends a valiant battle and a fine victory. To this class belong those who always have on their lips the great names of antiquity: they speak of that great Alexander, they proclaim Pyrrhus, king of the Epirots; what once happened to Furius Camillus; that Hannibal, the terror of Rome; Quintus Fabius, Marcus Marcellus, the one a shield, the other a sword of the Roman people. An inexperienced person in history, hearing such great names so often in academic orations, would rightly ask whether all these men were teachers, or masters of arts. Some of these names have been so cheapened by excessive use in France that, unless someone wishes to be hissed off the stage, he dares not call Cambyses or Epaminondas by name in a speech; if on occasion one must speak of them, one must use a periphrasis. Martial wittily mocks this abuse of great names on a small matter in his epigram against Postumus.

units.la: Caussidicum,
units.tr: The pleader:

units.la: Non de vi neque cæde nec veneno, Sed lis est mihi de tribus capellis. Vicini queror has abesse furto. Hoc judex sibi postulat probari: Tu Cannas, Mithridaticumque bellum, Et periuria Punici furoris, Et Syllas, Marioque, Mutioque, Magna voce sonas, manuque tota. Jam dic, Postume, de tribus capellis.
units.tr: It is not about violence, nor murder, nor poison. My suit is about three goats. I complain that my neighbour has these taken from me by theft. The judge demands that this be proved to him. You thunder out Cannae, the Mithridatic war, the perjuries of Punic fury, Sulla, Marius and Mucius, with a loud voice and your whole hand. Now tell us, Postumus, about the three goats.

units.la: Huic vitio vicinum est illud aliorum, qui, ut plus majestatis habeat oratio, levissima quæque, quæ nemo ignorare potest, magni alicujus ex antiquitate Viri auctoritate comprobant, quasi vero non liceret dicere, solem lucere, nisi ante idem Alphonsus Arragonia Rex, aut Agesilaus interrogatus dixisset. Qui quidem oratores sæpe non minus risu digni sunt, atque ille esset, qui in Convivio sodales ad hilaritatem excitaturus, ita graviter ordiretur: Non minus vere quam eleganter Venusinus Olor: Nunc, inquit, est bibendum. Magnam præterea orationem parvis rebus aptant; quorum in comœdiis servus loquitur, ut Oedipus in Tragœdia: in quorum Eclogis Tityrus loquitur, ut Æneas: in quorum Tragœdiis nutrix cum Medea de sublimitate sententiarumque magnificentiâ certare videtur: qui in elegiâ ita flent, ut Hercules furens bacchatur; qui in epistolis familiaribus ita loquuntur, tanquam si in senatu aut pro rostris dicerent: qui colloquia fingunt, qualia cum Diis sunt Sibyllarum, quoties oracula consulunt. Et quis omnes in hanc partem peccantes enumeraret?
units.tr: A fault close to this is that of those who, to lend their speech more dignity, back up the most trivial matters, which anyone can know, with the authority of some great man from antiquity, as if one could not say the sun shines unless King Alphonso of Aragon or Agesilaus, when asked, had said it first. Such speakers are often no less ridiculous than a man who, wanting to rouse his drinking companions to good cheer, began so solemnly: Not less truly than elegantly, the Venusian Swan says: Now, he says, we must drink. They also fit a grand style to small matters. In comedies a slave speaks as Oedipus does in tragedy; in eclogues Tityrus speaks as Aeneas does; in tragedies a nurse seems to vie with Medea in lofty sentiment and grandeur of thought; in an elegy they weep as furiously as Hercules raging; in familiar letters they write as if they were speaking in the Senate or from the Rostra; in dialogues they invent the kind of talk the Sibyls have with the gods whenever they consult their oracles. And who could list all who offend in this way?

units.la: X. Alterum meteori genus non in eo peccat, quod humili argumento orationem magnificam, infanti, ut loquuntur, Herculis cothurnos aptat, sed quod in grandi argumento, vitiosa fit sublimitas orationis: Ita omne illud voco, quod quibusdam sublime videtur, sed revera non est. Quo in genere peccant primò ii, quibus sublime omne id est, quod est obscurum. Quære ex his, quinam oratores sint maxime sublimes, Panegyricos Caſarum aut Tertullianum nominabunt, aut recentiores quosdam horum imitatores. Quid Cicero? Quem tu mihi Ciceronem narras, cujus oratio vel à pueris intelligitur? In historia longè Tacitus Livio est sublimior; quoniam hic longè facilius intelligitur. In Satyra Persius regnat, qui vix post tot doctissimorum virorum commentarios capi potest. Mirantur, in Epico carmine Virgilio primas tribui, qui multo est intellectu facilior Lucano, Statio, Claudiano, Prudentio, & hodiernis quamplurimis. Horatii odas contemnunt, quamdiu capiunt, tum demum Poetam admirantur, cum ex conspectu suo se subducit: tum vero sublimis, tum alter Pindarus est. Mirari aliquis posset, unde hoc hominibus in mentem venire potuerit, ut & ipsi in obscuritate gloriam quaerent, & aliorum obscuritatem admirarentur, cum oratio nobis non ad obscuranda, sed ad patefacienda animi sensa data sit? Multas hic error caussas habet. Praeterquam enim, quod semper ea majora habentur, quae latent: existimant quidam, auctorem, qui librum suum intelligit, te, qui non intelligis, necessario hoc ipso esse superiorem; capit enim, quod tu non capis; alii, quia in pueritia scriptores verè sublimes intelligere non potuerunt, assueverunt jam in scholis obscuri & sublimis notionem confundere: quod & iis accidit, qui admirantur auctores grandes illos quidem sed simul intellectu difficiles: solemus enim in iis, quos admiramur, promiscue virtutes & vitia admirari: alij denique magnitudinem ingenii, atque eruditionis, quae ab interpretibus ad intelligentiam obscuri auctoris requiritur, ad ipsum auctorem transferunt? Quantum est illud, quod vix Heinsii, Casauboni, Grotii, Salmasii, Scaligeri intelligere potuerunt? In quam sententiam memini cujusdam eloquentiam his verbis mihi jactantis: Quid tu? ait, nostine illum, nominabat hominem in humanioribus literis apprime versatum: doctum prædicant & ingeniosum: nostin? (sed nihil ad me.) Scripsi ad eum his diebus literas, quas vellem vidisses. Venio ad hominem postridie: ecquid literas meas acceperit, rogo. Annuit, sed quid mihi vellem his literis quaerit: quasi vero, inquam, tu illas non intelligas: tum vero ille dejerare, se ne verbulum quidem capere: ego hominis misereri, dicta explicare. Quid multis? coactus est denique fateri, se, nisi venissem, nihil horum, quae dicere volebam, unquam fuisse divinaturum. Haec cum dixisset homo sublimis eloquentiae, ridens me aspexit: & ego ridebam; uter nostrum graviores ridendi caussas habuerit,alij velim judicent. Ad has caussas affectatæ obscuritatis, si accedit ineptus præceptor, qui discipulis illud σκο-τισον,σκοτισον[?], ubique inculcat, qui illis obscurissimos quosque scriptores,ut nimirum illos videatur intelligere, præ cæteris commendat,qui discipulos propter obscuritatem laudat: tanto melius,ne ipse quidem intellexi; facile quilibet videt, unde tanta obscuritatis veniat reverentia: At non necesse erat tenebras in oratione quærere,vix vitari possunt, cum summo studio illas vitamus; quod tot optimorum Scriptorum exempla docent; in sublimi præsertim genere dicendi, cum & grandia , & grandibus verbis dicere volumus.
units.tr: X. Another kind of meteor does not lie in clothing a humble subject in a magnificent style, putting the buskin of Hercules on an infant, as the saying goes. Its fault is that, with a weighty subject, the speech becomes faulty sublimity. I call everything that seems lofty to some but is not really so by this name. Those who commit this fault first are those for whom everything is sublime that is obscure. Ask them which orators are the most sublime, and they will name the Panegyrics of the Caesars, or Tertullian, or some modern imitators of these. And Cicero? What Cicero do you mean to tell me about, whose speech is understood even by boys? In history, Tacitus is far more sublime than Livy, because the latter is far easier to understand. In satire, Persius reigns, though he can scarcely be grasped even after so many learned commentaries. They marvel that Virgil is given first place in epic poetry, though he is much easier to understand than Lucan, Statius, Claudian, Prudentius, and very many moderns. They despise the odes of Horace as long as they understand them, and only admire the poet when he withdraws from their sight; then, indeed, he is sublime, then he is another Pindar. One might wonder how people came to think this, that they should seek glory in obscurity and admire the obscurity of others, when speech was given us not to obscure but to reveal the feelings of the mind. This error has many causes. Besides the fact that what lies hidden is always thought greater, some believe that the author, who understands his own book while you do not, is for that very reason superior to you; he grasps what you do not grasp. Others, because as boys they could not understand truly sublime writers, have grown used to confusing obscurity with sublimity in the schools. This also happens to those who admire great authors who are at the same time difficult to understand, for we are wont to admire indiscriminately the virtues and the faults of those we admire. Finally, some transfer to the author himself the greatness of mind and learning that interpreters need in order to understand an obscure writer. How great is that which Heinsius, Casaubon, Grotius, Salmasius and Scaliger could scarcely understand! I recall a certain man boasting of his eloquence to me with these words: "What do you think? Do you know him," he said, naming a man thoroughly versed in the humane letters, "they call him learned and clever, do you know him? (But that is nothing to me.) I wrote him a letter these past days, which I wished you had seen. I went to see the man the next day and asked whether he had received my letter. He nodded, but asked what I wished to say in these letters. As if, I said, you did not understand them! Then he swore that he could not grasp even a single word. I felt sorry for the man and explained what I had said. In short, he was finally forced to confess that, had I not come, he would never have guessed any of the things I wanted to say." When this man of sublime eloquence had finished, he looked at me laughing, and I laughed too. Let others judge which of us had the graver reasons for laughter. To these causes of affected obscurity, add an inept teacher who constantly drums into his pupils "Obscure it! Obscure it!" [σκότισον, σκότισον], who recommends above all others the most obscure writers, as if he himself understood them, and who praises his pupils for their obscurity: "So much the better, I did not understand it myself either." Anyone can easily see where such reverence for obscurity comes from. Yet it was not necessary to seek darkness in speech, which can scarcely be avoided even when we take the greatest pains to avoid it; the examples of so many excellent writers show this, especially in the sublime style of speaking, when we wish to say great things in great words.

units.la: Cum enim magnam in mente rei imaginem formare conamur, sæpenumero tot tantaque iinagine nostra simul complecti volumus, ut imaginatio turbetur & confundatur, ipsique adeo, quid imaginemur, nesciamus; quod necessario obscurani[?] & confusam parit orationem.
units.tr: For when we try to form a great image of a thing in our mind, we often want to grasp so many great things at once in our imagination that the imagination becomes disturbed and confused, and we ourselves do not know what we are imagining. This necessarily produces an obscure and confused speech.

units.la: Nonnunquam imagine in mente recte formata, verba grandia desunt, quæ cum nimis longe petimus, non intelligimur. Nonnunquam nimis grandem sensum verbis nimis paucis, ad augendam orationis vim, exprimere volumus; quod si raro fit & fit, salvâ orationis perspicuitate, summam affert ei sublimitatem: sed quam facilis fit inde in obscuritatem lapsus, Taciti exemplum declarat. Excusanda hæc sunt in magnis scriptoribus, non imitanda, præsertim ab ijs, qui nonnihil vitia eorum imitari possunt.
units.tr: Sometimes, when the image is rightly formed in the mind, the great words are lacking, and when we seek them from too far off, we are not understood. Sometimes we wish to express a very great meaning in very few words in order to increase the force of the speech. If this is done rarely, and without loss of clarity, it gives the speech a high sublimity; but how easily one slips from there into obscurity, the example of Tacitus shows. Such things are to be excused in great writers, not imitated, especially by those who can imitate their faults a little.

units.la: XI. Sed & illi meteora tanquam sublimia captant, quibus omne id sublime videtur, quod est insolens, rarum, atque extraordinarium. His sordent omnia verba, omnes loquendi formæ vulgares & consuetæ. Cum legunt scriptores, ea tantum observant, quæ raro, aut, ut loqui solent, rarenter occurrunt. Fastidiunt fere Ciceronem, Cæsarem, Cornelium Nepotem, Terentium; nihil in horum libris est, quod excerpas. Quanto his Barclajus sublimior? quantus ex hoc auctore colligi potest rarissimarum vocum, phrasium, ut loquuntur, formularum, sententiarum, troporum, figurarum thesaurus. In Poëtis etiam præsertim hodiernis multa rara; In præfationibus vero librorum, in Inscriptionibus, in programmatibus, quot phrases occurrunt, cedro digna & auro contra cara. Tot phrasium raritatibus, ex omnium seculorum Poetis, Oratoribus, Philosophis, magno numero congestis, tandem stylus formatur, similis cimeliarchio, quo nonnisi rara naturæ & artis asservari solent. Hi homines nunquam ita se abjicient, ut Ciceronem, Ciceronem vocent: Arpinas noster ex libro phrasium est vocandus: Plautus, familiaris noster Sarsinas, Horatius nunquam Horatius est, sed Venusinus Cygnus; hunc si forte cum Virgilio comparant, dicent, se lachrymas & suspiria inter se comparare. Quantumcumque nomen Homeri sit, nunquam tamen Homerus est vocandus, sed ex Horatio, is qui nil molitur inepte. Loquere cum his de Martiali; quærent an Bilbilitanum argutatorem velis dicere. Erras, si hos unquam vinum bibere aut panem edere putas: Bacchi munera hauriunt, Cererem consumunt. Quid quæris? Omnes communes loquendi formas Spaniologi isti cane pejus & angue, sic enim loquuntur, fugiunt, & plusquam Vatiniano odio prosequuntur; & ne quidem cum Deo nisi ex Viridario aut ex formularum libro loqui possunt. Sed errant, quibus rariora semper sublimiora videntur: aliter sensit C. Cæsar, qui verbum insolens tanquam scopulum fugiendum esse censuit. Rara quoque sunt monstra, sed non ideo pulchra: Rari nani, sed non ideo grandes. Illis Plauti; ipsissimus, geminissimus, exclufissimus, occisissimus, fycolatronida, argentiexterebronida, fustitudinea, ferricrepina insula, quæ ad risum captandum confiƈta sunt, in oratione sublimi uti velle, quis non videt esse ridiculum? Qui Alexandrum ubique Pellaum juvenem, Aristotelem Stagyritam vocant; magnifice sibi loqui videntur, quasi Alexandri & Aristotelis nomina non essent grandiora. Magnopere videlicet Carolum V. Imperatorem & Henricum IV. Galliæ Regem extolleret, qui alterum Gandensem juvenem alterum Bearnensem appellaret? Grandius se loqui existimat, qui Pindarum, Thebana lyra fidicinem, quam qui Pindarum dicit, qui tamen ipse mallet Pindarus, quàm fidicen vocari. Sunt, quos nullis conditionibus permoveres, ut dicerent: Omnibus hoc notum est; malunt ex formularum libro: Et lippis & tonsoribus est notum: at lippi hi cum suis tonsoribus illustri præsentia magnificam orationem non valde condecorant. Alij magnopere sibi extollere videntur quaslibet res, si tantum eas inter cæteras teras sui generis caput efferre dicunt, Quantum lenta solent inter viburna cupressi: neque animadvertunt, hominem agrestem apud Virgilium ita loqui, cui campis, pratis atque arboribus nihil prius est. Ita tropi quoque, tametsi propriis verbis sint rariores, non ideo semper sunt sublimiores. Iniqua saepe conditione propria cum alienis permutamus, plusque est in hac permutatione jacturae quam lucri. Qui de excellentia hominis loquuntur, non augent orationem, si eum non trita voce hominem, sed mortalem vocant. Qui toties de mundi fornicibus loquuntur, plus dicerent si caelum caelum vocarent. Qui caelum buccinare ait, longe minus dicit, quam si proprie tonare diceret. Qui mare appellavit fossam ponti, significantiore usus esset verbo, si quotidianum maris nomen retinuisset. Ita nihil in permutatione vocum lucri capiunt, qui terram cum terra pila, mare cum Neptunia lacuna, equum cum ungula, domum cum nido, majus cum minori, significantius cum minus significanti permutant vocabulo. Addere possumus honestum cum turpi & obscaenorum: ut sunt, nubes Varronis aquam vomentes, Furij Jupiter Alpes nive conspuens: de quibus sapienter Cicero: Quoniam hac vel summa, inquit, lex est verbi transferendi, ut sensum feriat id, quod translatum sit, fugienda est omnis turpitudo earum rerum, ad quas eorum animos, qui audiunt, trahet similitudo. Nolo morte Africani captam esse Rempubl. nolo stercus Curiae dici Glanciam. Quamvis sit simile, tamen est in utroque deformis cogitatio similitudinis. Viderint igitur, quam magnifice loquantur, quibus: maledicta evomere, blasphemias eructare, in patrios cineres mingere, cacata charta, judaeis curtis oppedere, & aliae hujusmodi munditiae tantopere placent.
units.tr: XI. But there are also those who pursue meteors as if they were sublime, for whom everything seems sublime that is unusual, rare, and extraordinary. Every common word seems mean to them, every ordinary and customary form of speech. When they read authors, they note only what occurs rarely, or, as they say, rarely. They nearly despise Cicero, Caesar, Cornelius Nepos, Terence; there is nothing in their books that you would want to excerpt. How much more sublime is Barclay! How rich a treasure of the rarest words, phrases, as they say, formulas, sentiments, tropes and figures can be gathered from this author! In poets, especially modern ones, there is much that is rare; but in the prefaces of books, in inscriptions and programmes, how many phrases occur that are worthy of cedar and dearer than gold! When the style is formed from such a heap of rare phrases, gathered in great numbers from poets, orators and philosophers of all ages, it becomes like a cabinet in which only the rare products of nature and art are usually kept. These men will never so far lower themselves as to call him Cicero, Cicero; he must be called our Arpinate from a phrase book; Plautus, our familiar Sarsinate; Horace is never Horace but the Venusian Swan. If by chance you compare him with Virgil, they will say that they are comparing tears and sighs with each other. However famous the name of Homer may be, he must never be called Homer, but, from Horace, he who attempts nothing foolishly. Speak with them about Martial; they will ask whether you wish to call him the Bilbilitan wrangler. You are mistaken if you think they ever drink wine or eat bread: they drink the gifts of Bacchus, they consume Ceres. What more do you want? Those Spanish-speakers hate all common forms of speech worse than dog or snake, for so they speak, they flee them, and pursue them with more than Vatinian hatred; nor can they speak even with God except from a pleasure garden or a book of formulas. But those err for whom the rarer things always seem more sublime. Caesar thought otherwise, holding that an unusual word must be avoided like a rock. Monsters are also rare, but not for that reason beautiful; dwarfs are rare, but not for that reason great. Who does not see that it is ridiculous to want to use in lofty speech those words of Plautus, ipsissimus, geminissimus, exclufissimus, occisissimus, fycolatronida, argentiexterebronida, fustitudinea, ferricrepina insula, which were invented to catch laughter? Those who call Alexander everywhere the young man of Pella and Aristotle the Stagirite seem to themselves to speak magnificently, as if the names of Alexander and Aristotle were not grander already. Would one indeed exalt the Emperor Charles V and Henry IV, King of France, greatly by calling the one the young man of Ghent and the other the Bearnese? He thinks he speaks more grandly who calls Pindar the lyre-player of Thebes, than he who simply says Pindar, though Pindar himself would rather be called Pindar than lyre-player. There are some whom no conditions could move to say: This is known to everyone; they prefer, from the formula book, It is known both to the bleary-eyed and to the barbers. But these bleary-eyed men, with their barbers, do not greatly adorn a magnificent speech with such illustrious company. Others seem to exalt to themselves whatever things they say rise above all others of their kind, as the slender cypress rises among the viburnums, and do not notice that this is how a country man speaks in Virgil, for whom nothing is more important than fields, meadows and trees. So too tropes, though rarer than proper words, are not therefore always more sublime. We often exchange the proper with the foreign on unfavourable terms, and in this exchange there is more loss than gain. Those who speak of the excellence of a man do not enlarge their speech if they call him a mortal rather than using the common word for man. Those who so often speak of the vaults of the world would say more if they called heaven heaven. He who says that the sky trumpets says far less than if he said it thunders. He who called the sea the ditch of the sea would have used a more expressive word if he had kept the everyday name for the sea. Thus those who exchange earth for earthen ball, sea for Neptunian pool, horse for hoof, house for nest, the greater for the lesser, the more significant for the less significant word, gain nothing by such exchanges. We may add the honourable exchanged for the base and obscene: such as Varro's clouds vomiting water, and Furius's Jupiter spitting Alps with snow. Of these Cicero wisely said: Since this is the highest law of transferred words, that what is transferred should strike the sense, all baseness must be avoided in those things to which the likeness will draw the minds of the hearers. I do not want the Republic to be said to have been taken by the death of Africanus, nor Glaucia to be called the dung of the Curia. Although the likeness is there, the thought of the likeness is ugly in both cases. Let them see, then, how magnificently speak those who take such delight in vomiting curses, belching blasphemies, pissing on their fathers' ashes, cacata charta, and tearing at the Jews with short claws, and other such elegancies of this kind.

units.la: XII. Neque illi [?] in Oratione & sublime distinguunt, qui nimis exquisitum in sublimi oratione affectant ornatum. Periodos ubique quaerunt probe mensuratas, omnia cola & incisa apte sibi respondentia, libratas plurium membrorum antitheses & comparationes, earum aequales itus reditusque, voces sonosque ad numerum repetitos, similiter incipientia & cadentia, rotundas sententiolas, clausulas inexpectatas, argutos lusus in similibus, oppositis, aut verborum ambiguitatibus, dicta factaque veterum, fabulas[?], totamque rerum naturam per ingeniosam allegoriam ad argumentum suum tractam, ne dicam tortam. Horum quaedam si modice adhibentur in oratione ad delectationem composita, aliquid venustatis habent: si frequentantur, inepta vel in ludicra oratione, at in gravi & sublimi monstra sunt non ferenda, neque magis decent, quam si vir gravis in concione populi ad numerum saltare vellet. Romani Augusti aevo has delicias non magnopere captabant; solus Ovidius his interdum lusibus delectari videtur: Tempore vero Neronis frequentari coeperunt, quod Senecarum scripta demonstrant: ac paulo post tota eloquentia in his ponebatur, ut Petronii & Quintiliani docent querela. Inde transiit haec dicendi consuetudo in Ecclesiam. Non pudet, inquit Hieronymus, Christianos & Sacerdotes Dei, quasi de rebus ludicris agatur, verbis dubiis haerere, & ambiguas librare sententias, quibus loquens magis quam audiens decipitur. Multorum Ecclesiae Patrum scripta his lusibus plena: a quibus eadem dicendi ratio ad nostra usque tempora manavit, quam tanta fide sacri quidam Oratores retinent, ut nullus dubitem, eos hanc consuetudinem posteris quoque esse tradituros. Ubi dolendum est, in iis orationibus maxime ludi, ubi minime ludi oportebat. Haec vel aptissime summoque cum judicio adhibita orationem aliquando venustiorem reddunt, nunquam sublimiorem & grandiorem; atque adeo tantum Orationi gravitatis detrahunt, quantum addunt venustatis. Recte Demetrius: ἡ ὁμοιότης ἡ [?] τὰ κα- λὰ καὶ ἡ ἀντίθεσις ἐκλύει τὴν [?]. Id de omnibus hujus generis pigmentis dici potest. Exemplo sit elegantissimum illud de Didonis Interitu Epigramma:
units.tr: XII. Nor do those distinguish well in oratory between the lofty and the elevated who, in a sublime speech, aim at exquisite ornament. Everywhere they look for periods carefully measured, all cola and incisa aptly corresponding to one another, antitheses and comparisons of several balanced members, their equal goings and returns, voices and sounds repeated in rhythm, beginning and ending alike, rounded little maxims, unexpected closing clauses, clever plays on similar and opposite words, or on ambiguities of words, sayings and deeds of the ancients, fables, and the whole of nature brought into their subject through a clever allegory, not to say a twisted one. If some of these are used sparingly in a speech composed for pleasure, they have some charm. If they are used often, they are out of place even in a playful speech, but in a grave and lofty one they are monsters that cannot be tolerated, and they suit it no better than if a serious man wished to dance in rhythm before the people at a sermon. In the age of Augustus the Romans did not greatly pursue these delights; only Ovid seems to have sometimes enjoyed such games. In the time of Nero they began to be frequent, as the writings of Seneca show; and a little later the whole of eloquence was placed in them, as the complaints of Petronius and Quintilian teach. From there this manner of speaking passed into the Church. It is not shameful, says Jerome, for Christians and priests of God, as if the matter were a trifle, to cling to doubtful words and weigh out ambiguous sentences, by which the speaker is deceived more than the hearer. The writings of many Fathers of the Church are full of these games, and from them the same manner of speaking has flowed down even to our own times, which some holy orators hold so faithfully that I doubt not they will hand this custom on to posterity too. Here it is to be lamented that the games are greatest where there ought to be least play. These devices, if applied most aptly and with the greatest judgement, sometimes make a speech more graceful, but never more lofty and grand; and so they take away as much gravity from the oration as they add charm. Demetrius rightly says: [ἡ ὁμοιότης ἡ ... τὰ καλὰ καὶ ἡ ἀντίθεσις ἐκλύει τὴν ...] the likeness ... and the antithesis weakens the ... This can be said of all pigments of this kind. Let the most elegant epigram on the death of Dido serve as an example:

units.la: Infelix Dido, nulli bene nupta marito: Hoc pereunte fugis, hoc fugiente peris.
units.tr: Unhappy Dido, never well married to any husband: by her dying you flee, by her fleeing you perish.

units.la: Nihil venustius est, sed & nihil minus sublime: hoc enim quisquis legit, non Didonis interitum miseratur, sed Poetae argutiam miratur: ἀντιθέσεως concinnitas, tamque apta commutatio verborum fugere & perire facit, ut Didonis tantum non oblivisca-mur. Augustinus certe, qui lecto quarto libro Æneidos Virgilianae mortem Didonis lachrymis prosecutus est, siccis hoc Epigramma oculis legisset.
units.tr: Nothing is more graceful, but nothing is less lofty. For whoever reads this does not pity Dido's death but admires the cleverness of the poet: the neatness of the antithesis and so apt a shift of words make you flee and perish, so that we almost forget Dido. Augustine certainly, who after reading the fourth book of Virgil's Aeneid wept over Dido's death, would have read this epigram with dry eyes.

units.la: XIII. Convenit quidem sublimi dictioni parcior ornatus, sed non ubique: Quod si enim imago rei, quam mente concepimus, vere magna est, tanto major videbitur, quo simplicioribus eam verbis exprimimus: prorsus quemadmodum eximia pulchritudo vestibus elegantissimis non tam ornatur quam tegitur: cibus exquisiti saporis multis condimentis corrumpitur, suavissimumque melos nimijs vocis modulationibus redditur deterius; denique omne id, quod nudum & simplex optimum est, tale si relinquatur, est gratissimum. Illud Genesis: Dixit Deus fiat lux & facta est lux, fiat terra, & facta est terra; Cujus dicti sublimitatem tantopere Longinus deprædicat, ideo tam sublime est, quia tam simplex. Quod si vero quædam in oratione sublimi verbis ornanda sunt; danda est opera, ut nullus, quantum fieri poterit, ornatus appareat, nusquam enim minus conspicuus esse debet. Poscunt Architecturæ regulæ, ut columnæ ornatus gratia splendidis ædibus additæ, necessitatis causa, ad fulciendum ædificij pondus, illi substructæ esse videantur: Ita & in Oratione idipsum quod ornat, non ornatus causa quæsitum, sed ad pondus sententiæ nostræ sustinendum necessario dictum esse videatur. Talis denique in ornatu modus adhibeatur, ne auditorem ab illo affectu, quem in eo concitare volumus, ad orationis venustatem admirandam aliasque cogitationes avocemus. Id quod faciunt illi, qui, ut ait Quintilianus, sententiolas flent, aut Periodis postulant, itaque nihil aliud dicendo consequuntur, quam ut, qui his capiuntur, dicant, elegantem se audivisse orationem; cæterum dictis neque moventur neque mutantur.
units.tr: XIII. A sparer ornament indeed suits lofty diction, but not everywhere.
