For if the image of a thing which we have conceived in the mind is truly great, it will appear all the greater the more simply we express it in words. Just as exquisite beauty is not so much adorned as covered by the most elegant garments; food of exquisite flavour is spoiled by many seasonings, and the sweetest song is made worse by excessive modulations of the voice; in short, whatever is best when bare and simple, if it is left so, is most pleasing. Take that passage in Genesis: God said, let there be light, and there was light; let there be earth, and there was earth. Longinus extols the sublimity of this saying so highly, and it is sublime precisely because it is so simple. But if some things in a lofty speech must indeed be adorned with words, care must be taken that no ornament, as far as possible, appears; for it should be nowhere less conspicuous. The rules of architecture require that a column added to a splendid building for the sake of ornament should seem to be placed beneath it out of necessity, to support the weight of the structure. So too in speech, that which adorns should seem to have been said by necessity, not sought for the sake of ornament, but to bear the weight of our sentence. Finally, let such a measure be observed in ornament that we do not draw the hearer away from that emotion which we wish to stir in him to admire the elegance of the speech and other thoughts. This is what those do who, as Quintilian says, weep over little maxims or demand periods; and so they achieve nothing by speaking except that those who are captivated by them say they have heard an elegant speech, but they are neither moved nor changed by what was said.

units.la: XIV. Huc pertinent quoque, quas adeo multi affectant, periphrases, quæ non semper plus sensus habenr, ut plus habent verborum, nisi forte magnifice is de Cicerone locutus est, qui illum Romanorum aromatum Myropolam vocavit. Sed & minus ineptæ enervant sæpius orationem quam augent, sicq; ut propter verborum multitudinem sententiæ vis ac sublimitas non conspiciatur. Quam sublime est illud Virgilij:
units.tr: XIV. To this belongs also the periphrasis, which so many affect; it does not always have more meaning, though it has more words. Unless perhaps the speaker of Cicero spoke grandly when he called him the perfumer-shop of Roman spices. But even the less absurd periphrases often weaken a speech rather than enlarge it, so that because of the multitude of words the force and sublimity of the thought is not seen. How sublime is that line of Virgil:

units.la: Et campus ubi Troja fuit.
units.tr: And the plain where Troy was.

units.la: Da periphrastice, ut Præceptor clamat, magna sublimitatis pars evanescet. Quid illud Lucani excusantis Romæ univerfæ, Cæsare adventante, terrorem, quem cum magnifice descripsisset, subjicit:
units.tr: Say it periphrastically, as the teacher shouts, and a great part of the sublimity vanishes. Consider that passage of Lucan, where, after describing with grandeur the terror of all Rome at Caesar's approach, he adds:

units.la: Danda tamen venia est tantorum danda pavorum, Pompejo fugiente timent.
units.tr: Yet pardon must be given for such great terrors; they fear while Pompey flees.

units.la: tribus his verbis plus dixit Poëta, quam si omnem Pompeji magnitudinem, si fugam ipsius magno verborum ambitu descripsisset. Id quod ijs etiam dictum esse volo, qui nullum nomen, ut loquuntur, substantivum solum incedere patiuntur, sed omnia honoris causa splendido epitheтo[?] comitantur.
units.tr: In these three words the poet said more than if he had described all of Pompey's greatness and his flight with a great array of words. I wish this said also to those who allow no noun, as they say, to walk alone, but accompany every word with a splendid epithet for the sake of honour.

units.la: X V. At nec illi in Oratione μετέωρον & sublime discernunt, qui dictionis sublimitatem ponunt in grande quiddam sonantibus vocibus, ac magnifica & nescio quid promittente verborum grandium nihil magni significantium structura. In Poëtis id appellat Horatius:
units.tr: XV. Nor do those distinguish well in oratory between the meteoron [μετέωρον] and the lofty, who place the sublimity of diction in something grand in sound, in resounding words, and in a structure of grand words that promises I know not what and signifies nothing great. Horace calls this, in poets:

units.la: Versus inopes rerum nugasque canoras.
units.tr: Verses empty of matter and tuneful trifles.

units.la: Qui hæc affectant, aut nesciunt in quo vera orationis granditas consistat, aut ingenio destituti, illam cum assequi non possint, magnam sibi sonantium verborum copiam comparant, quibus ingenij parvitatem utcunque tegant, ut quidam splendore vestium paupertatem. Hi non magnopere solliciti sunt quid dicant, aut num omnino aliquid dicant, dummodo possint Orationem, ut Sedulij, magni in hac arte Magistri, verbis utar,
units.tr: Those who aim at these things either do not know in what the true grandeur of speech consists, or, lacking talent and unable to attain it, procure for themselves a great store of resounding words, with which they somehow hide the smallness of their wit, as some hide poverty by the splendour of their clothes. These men are not much concerned about what they say, or whether they say anything at all, provided they can, to use the words of Sedulius, that great master of this art, strut in grandiloquent measures and tragic roar,

units.la: Grandisonis pompare modis tragicoque boatu dummodo verba sint, resonantia, undantia, rorantia, rutilantia, radiantia flammantia, corruscantia, tumultuantia, bacchantia, quadrupedantia. Hæc verba parum aut nihil significent: dummodo tonent, fulgurent, fulminent, late grassentur, quaquaversum omnia quatiant, perrumpant, proruant. Sit sensus humilis; dum verba sint aurata, marmorea, turrita, fastigiata. Nihil in oratione cohæreat, dum in ea compareat bosphorus, campi hyperborei, æstuantis Adria sinus, Carpathium pelagus, cum in hospitali Caucaso & Acroceraunijs. Tantorum verborum sono quis non deciperetur, ut existimaret, sublime esse in Oratione, quod, si sensum quæret, non nisi μετέωρον esse videbit. Hæc fere est causa, quare multi sequioris ævi Poëtas ijs, qui Augusti tempore & ante floruerunt, tanquam grandiores anteponunt. Hi Claudianum libros de raptu Proserpina longe sublimiore stylo incipere dicent, quam Virgilius Æneida, aut Ovidius metamorphoses orditur. Ita enim ille:
units.tr: provided only the words are resounding, surging, dewy, glittering, radiant, flaming, flashing, tumultuous, raging, four-footed. These words signify little or nothing: provided they thunder, lighten, hurl bolts, rage far and wide, shake everything on every side, burst through, and overthrow. Let the sense be low, provided the words are gilded, marble, turreted, pinnacled. Let nothing in the speech hang together, provided there appear the Bosphorus, the Hyperborean plains, the seething gulf of the Adriatic, the Carpathian sea, along with the hospitable Caucasus and the Acroceraunian crags. Who would not be deceived by the sound of such great words and think that what is lofty in the speech, when he seeks the sense, will be seen to be nothing but meteoron? This is roughly the reason why many poets of a later age are preferred by some as grander than those who flourished in the time of Augustus and before. They will say that the books of Claudian on the rape of Proserpina begin in a far more elevated style than Virgil begins his Aeneid, or Ovid his Metamorphoses. For he says:

units.la: Inferni raptoris equos, afflataque currus Sidera Tanario,caligantesque profunda Junonis thalamos audaci promere cantu Mens congesta jubet.
units.tr: The steeds of the infernal ravisher, and the chariot breathed upon by Tanarus' stars, and the shadowy bridal chambers of deep Juno, my mind, gathered together, bids me bring forth in bold song.

units.la: Videamus hoc exemplo, an non verborum granditas lectori fucum facere possit, ut majus quam quod legit, sibi legere videatur. Ambitiosa illa epitheta: Raptor infernus, currus Tanarius, thalami caligantes, juno profunda, cantus audax & mens congesta plus sonant, quam significant. Quomodo interpretabimur ista: mens congesta jubet promere, aut prodere, ut alij legunt, cantu equos & sidera curru afflata? Maluissem, Poeta nobis cecinisset, infandum Plutonis facinus, crudeles horrendi raptoris manus, durissima brachia, quae Jovis filiam, unicum Cereris delicium, Deam perpetua luce dignam, nequicquam PatremMatremque implorantem, corripuerunt, comprehensamque per immanes specus ad aeternas secum tenebras traxerunt. Nihil horum in isto Claudiani exordio videmus: equi raptoris comparent, post currus sequitur: Proserpinam non conspicimus, nisi in thalamis, cum jam juno profunda est, fortasse ne rapta Proserpina commiseratione nos tangat. Hujus nuptiae thalami appellantur caligantes, qua in re Juno profunda non infelix videbitur illis, qui in his thalamis lucem non requirunt. Magnam igitur Poeta neque concepit, neque verbis expressit imaginem argumenti sui, in quo equi Plutonis, currus ejus & nuptiae Proserpinae minimum atrocitatis habent: Maximum in hoc raptu est ipse raptus. Similisque adeo pictori est Poeta, qui quadrigam nobis depingeret trahentem currum, quo homines velati veherentur: post in alia tabulae parte, tanquam in loco remotiore, lectum in tenebris, cum hac Inscriptione: Raptus Proserpina. Quanto rectius Ovidius orditur Metamorphoses:
units.tr: Let us see by this example whether the grandeur of the words cannot make a fog for the reader, so that he seems to himself to read something greater than what he reads. Those ambitious epithets: infernal ravisher, Tanarian chariot, shadowy bridal chambers, deep Juno, bold song and gathered mind make more sound than sense. How shall we construe these: my mind, gathered together, bids me bring forth, or, as others read, betray, in song the steeds and stars breathed upon by the chariot? I would have preferred that the poet sang for us the unspeakable deed of Pluto, the cruel hands of the dreadful ravisher, the hardest arms, which seized Jove's daughter, Ceres' only delight, a goddess worthy of perpetual light, who in vain called upon her father and mother, and dragged her, held fast, through huge caverns into eternal darkness with him. We see none of this in that opening of Claudian: the steeds of the ravisher appear, then the chariot follows; we do not catch sight of Proserpina except in the bridal chambers, when already deep Juno is there, perhaps so that the abducted Proserpina may not touch us with pity. Her wedding is called bridal chambers, shadowy, a thing in which deep Juno will seem not unhappy to those who do not seek light in these chambers. The poet therefore has neither conceived nor expressed in words a great image of his subject, in which the horses of Pluto, his chariot and the wedding of Proserpina have very little of horror; the greatest thing in this rape is the rape itself. The poet is like a painter who depicted for us a four-horse team drawing a chariot in which veiled men were carried, and then in another part of the panel, as if in a more distant place, a bed in shadows, with this inscription: The rape of Proserpina. How much more rightly Ovid begins his Metamorphoses:

units.la: In nova fert animus mutatas dicere formas corpora.
units.tr: My mind is moved to tell of bodies changed into new forms.

units.la: paucis verbis ijsque perspicuis omnem argumenti sui magnitudinem complectitur, ut de Aeneidos initio, secundique libri Lucretij, quo vix quicquam sublimius est, taceam. Caeterum, quod Claudiano contigit, quem non negamus ingentis spiritus Poetam fuisse, id si hodiernis quoque Poetis cum illo minime comparandis aliquando accidit, ut plus soni quam sensus habeant eorum carmina, minime est mirandum: facilius quippe est grandia verba ex Poetis, aut quod quidam faciunt, ex phrasium Poeticarum Thesauris excerpere, quam grandes sensus ex pectore depromere.
units.tr: In a few clear words he takes in the whole greatness of his subject. I say nothing of the opening of the Aeneid or of the second book of Lucretius, than which nothing is more sublime. But what happened to Claudian, whom we do not deny was a poet of great spirit, sometimes happens also to modern poets who are not to be compared with him at all: their poems have more sound than sense. This is hardly surprising, for it is easier to pick out grand words from the poets, or, as some do, from the storehouses of poetic phrases, than to draw grand thoughts from the heart.

units.la: XVI. Inter omnia vero μετέωρα nulla sunt, quae magis sublimitatis speciem mentiuntur, quam illa quae præcipitia Quintilianus, alii tumida, turgida & inflata appellant. Est autem tumor orationis nihil aliud, quam quidam granditatis excessus, in quem ijomnes prolabuntur, qui, cum imaginandi potius facultate, quam judicandi pollent, quoties magnifice dicere volunt, omnia quidem adhibent, quibus orationem sublimem fieri diximus, sed nusquam aut modum aut decorum servare possunt. Hi igitur si magnam rei in mente imaginem formare volunt, formant vastam; si sublimem, formant enormem; si admirabilem, formant portentosam prorsus & incredibilem. Cum procerum hominem concipere volunt, concipiunt gigantem: cum virum fortem, nescio quem fabulosum concipiunt Heroem. Grandem Cicero amicitiae imaginem animo complexus est: Non aqua, inquit, non igni, non aere pluribus locis utimur, quam amicitia: Si quis Ciceronem hic superaturus diceret: amicitia longe pluribus in locis utimur, quam aere, modum excederet. Magnam corrupti seculi ideam concipit; qui dicit, usque eo rem venisse, ut scelerum neminem pudeat, multi ijs etiam glorientur. Nimiam conciperet, si quis cum Seneca diceret: nullum intra se manet hodie vitium, adeo unusquisque sua amat, ut nolit peccare, nisi adsit testis. Qui hæc μέ-[?] τέωρα amant, ij in soluta oratione tantum nonnunquam imaginationi indulgent, quantum Poetae, imo quantum vix Poetis concederetur. Hos si audis, D. Brutus Gallaecos domuit, atque omnes Gallaecia populos, formidatumque militibus flumen oblivionis, peragratoque victor Oceani littore non prius signa convertit, quam cadentem in maria solem, obrutumque aquis ignem, non sine quodam sacrilegii metu & horrore deprehendit. Si temperatam describunt regionem: Nulla unquam nubes coelum asperat, nulla bruma segetes extinguit, nulli astus adurunt. Si sapientem laudant: Quovis ille adamante durior est: non modo nulli telo penetrabi-lis, sed ipsi etiam arietes & machina, qua altissimas turres prosternunt, munitissimas arces diruunt, hunc ne agitant quidem: firmior est Babylonis, Carthaginis, Numantiae ipsius denique Capitolii muris. Quantamcunque telorum multitudinem in eum conjicias, nullum eorum hominem tantum vulnerat, ferit, imo ne quidem attingit. Quemcunque aut Regem aut Principem extollere volunt: hic vero magis Alexander est & Caesar, quam ipse Alexander & Caesar fuerunt: & si quando crescit imaginationis fervor: totus mundus basis est nimis exigua ad imaginemejus [sustentandam: non satis in hoc universo papyri est, ad virtutesejus describendas: neque omnino calamo id peragi potest: solem has radius [suis] scribere oportet. In carmine vero, quid non audet concitata nulloque judicio frenata imaginatio; quia multa licent, omnia licere putat. Nihil tam vastum tam enorme, tam monstrosum est, quod non effundit. Nunc in nubibus est nunc in abysso, nunc extra mundum rapitur, coelum terramque miscet:
units.tr: XVI. Among all the faults of style there are none that more falsely wear the look of sublimity than those which Quintilian calls precipitia and others call tumida, turgida and inflata (swollen, bloated, puffed up). Now the swelling of style is nothing other than a certain excess of grandeur, into which all those fall who, being more gifted in imagination than in judgement, when they want to speak grandly, use indeed all the means by which, as we said, a style is made lofty, but nowhere can keep measure or propriety. If they want to form a great image of a thing in their mind, they form a vast one; if a lofty one, an enormous one; if a wonderful one, a portentous and utterly incredible one. When they wish to conceive a tall man, they conceive a giant; when a brave man, they conceive some legendary hero. Cicero embraced a grand image of friendship: We make use of fire, water and air in more places, he says, than of friendship. If someone wanting to outdo Cicero here said, We make use of friendship in far more places than of air, he would go beyond measure. He conceives a great idea of a corrupt age who says that things have come to such a pass that no one is ashamed of crimes, and many even boast of them. He would conceive an excessive one who said with Seneca: Nowadays no vice remains hidden within a man; everyone so loves himself that he would not sin unless a witness were present. Those who love these swellings indulge their imagination in prose only now and then, but as much as poets do, indeed as much as scarcely would be allowed to poets. If you listen to them, D. Brutus subdued the Gallaeci and all the peoples of Gallaecia and the river that the soldiers dreaded as the river of forgetfulness; and having travelled over the shore of the Ocean as victor, he did not turn back his standards until he saw the sun sinking into the sea and the fire quenched in the waters, not without a certain dread and horror of sacrilege. If they describe a temperate region: No cloud ever darkens the sky there, no winter ever destroys the crops, no heats ever scorch. If they praise a wise man: He is harder than any adamant: not only can he not be pierced by any weapon, but even rams and the engines by which men overthrow the loftiest towers and demolish the best-fortified citadels do not so much as touch him; he is firmer than the walls of Babylon, of Carthage, of Numantia, and of the Capitol itself. However great a multitude of weapons you hurl at him, none of them wounds or strikes the man, nay, none even touches him. Whichever king or prince they want to extol, this man is more of an Alexander and a Caesar than Alexander and Caesar themselves ever were; and when the heat of imagination rises: The whole world is too small a base to support his image: there is not enough paper in this whole universe to describe his virtues, nor can it be done at all with a pen: the sun's rays must be used to write them. In poetry, however, what does an excited imagination, curbed by no judgement, not dare? Since it thinks everything is permitted, it ventures on many things. Nothing is so vast, so enormous, so monstrous that it does not pour it out. Now it is in the clouds, now in the abyss, now it is carried beyond the world, it mingles heaven and earth:

units.la: Cum variare volet rem, prodigialiter unam, Delphinum sylvis appingit, fluctibus aprum.
units.tr: When he wants to vary a subject, he paints in prodigious fashion a dolphin in the woods and a boar in the waves.

units.la: Hic milites nobis adeo pugnae intentos narrat, ut etiam post mortem in pugnando perseverarint, non animadvertentes se mortuos esse: Hic aggerem, quem Poeta inter Zodiaci signa collocarent, nisi metuerent, ne firmitate & altitudine sua solis cursum impediret. Si tempestas describitur mare concutiens, quo non aufertur imaginatio? Venti bella gerunt: Aquilo vincit: hic non fluctus concitat, sed maria integra loco movet: commiscentur mare Ægeum & Tyrrhenum, Ionium & Adriaticum: Oceanus à reliquis ventis tenetur: terra denique omnis inundatur, mare est sine littore, coelo solo tenetur:
units.tr: Here he tells us of soldiers so intent on battle that they went on fighting even after death, not noticing that they were dead. Here is a mound which the poet would have placed among the signs of the Zodiac, were he not afraid that by its firmness and height it would hinder the course of the sun. If a storm is described as stirring the sea, where does the imagination not carry us? The winds wage war: the North Wind conquers; he does not merely stir the waves but moves the seas bodily from their place: the Aegean and Tyrrhenian seas, the Ionian and Adriatic, are mingled; the Ocean is held back by the other winds; in short, the whole earth is flooded, the sea has no shore, it is held up by the sky alone:

units.la: Tunc quoque tanta maris moles crevisset in astra, Ni superum rector pressisset nubibus undas.
units.tr: Then too the mass of the sea would have risen to the stars, had not the ruler of the gods pressed down the waters with clouds.

units.la: In sacro etiam argumento non minus imaginatio sibi permittit. Licuerit Homero nescio quae monstra Deorum fingere, Deos ab hominibus vulneratos, quod cum Marti contigisset, clamaverit bellator iste Deus,
units.tr: Even in a sacred subject imagination takes no less licence for itself. Homer was allowed to invent I know not what monstrous things about the gods, such as gods wounded by men; when this happened to Mars, that warlike god cried out

units.la: Ὅσον τ' ἐννεάχιλοι ἐπίαχον ἢ δεκάχιλοι.
units.tr: as loud as nine or ten thousand men shouting [Ὅσον τ' ἐννεάχιλοι ἐπίαχον ἢ δεκάχιλοι].

units.la: Neque enim certo id scit Poëta. Quis Christianum Poëtam feret, Christo nascente, hæc evenisse fingentem:
units.tr: For the poet did not know this for certain. Who would tolerate a Christian poet who pretends that these things happened when Christ was born?

units.la: stelliataque machina mundi Proscripsit ferale iubar, micuere fecundo Omine siderea facies: dum pignora cœlum Tanta sibi promissa putat: sua frigora fulgens Ægoceros media voluit mitescere bruma, Et tepuit glacialis hiems, decessit Olympo Arctophylax, fugit socia cum conjuge Cepheus Et Chiron Persëusque furens & Plejas & ipse Amphitryoniades.
units.tr: And the starry frame of the world cast out its deadly light; the sidereal face shone with a fruitful omen, while heaven thought such great pledges were promised to it. Capricorn, shining, wished his cold to soften in the middle of winter, and icy winter grew warm; the Charioteer's Bear departed from Olympus, Cepheus fled with his wife at his side, and Chiron, and furious Perseus, and the Pleiades, and Amphitryon's son himself.

units.la: Ut illam permixtionem religionis nostræ mysteriorum cum absurdissimis Gentilium fabulis, in qua tantum sibi Christiani Poëtæ nonnunquam indulgent, silentio præteream.
units.tr: I pass over in silence that mixing of the mysteries of our religion with the most absurd fables of the Gentiles, in which Christian poets sometimes indulge so freely.

units.la: XVII. Cum vero non in sensu tantum orationis, sed in verbis etiam sublimitatem quærunt ij, qui plus ingenij, quam judicij habent, quæ non verba, quas loquendi formas non adducunt[?]? Ad petendas metaphoras aliosque tropos ab uno mundi extremo ad aliud currunt; quæ sponte sequi nolunt, trahuntur: periphrases finguntur enormes, & non uno spiritu enuntiandæ: quicquid in hoc universo magnum est, cœlum cum plagis suis omnibusq; astris, omnes terræ earumque populi, omnia maria, lacus, flumina, montes, omnes Dij Deæque, omnia denique monstra nomina sua, cognomina atque epitheta scribenti commodare debent, ut his coacervatis granditas orationis augeatur. Neptuno tridens, Minervæ clypeus, cum capite Medusæ, Phœbo quadriga, Mercurio talares alæ, ipsi denique Herculi clava, imo Jovi trisulcum fulmen eripitur. Xerxes jam non amplius est Persarum Rex, sed Persarum Jupiter. Vultures jam non amplius aves sunt rapaces, sed sepulchra animata. Heliotropium florum est Mathusalemus. Qui lac equinum bibunt, illi ex cornipedis visceribus cibos extrahunt. Nullæ jam amplius in aere sagittæ volitant, sed pennatæ mortes athera sibi vindicant. Non jam amplius orator clamat, clamat, quid primum, quid deinde dicam? sed ita: Quas aristas horreis inferam, quas relinquam? En formulam oratoris Panegyrici ad finem orationis properantis: Vellem, fateor, ad orationis terminum victus gestorum tuorum enormitate describere & novellas adoreas, hebetatus priscorum luce, transire. Quemadmodum fi aetherei axis in numerum redigere ornamenta voluissem, & trionum fulgore comprehenso coeli decorem impotenti lingua describere, cederet divino splendori mortalis obscuritas, jubaris lampadi non sufficeret humilium scintilla sermonum. Denique ne singulae quidem voces, vulgares si sunt, placent; nulla satis dignitatis, aut soni, aut sensus habet. Novae fingendae, veteres revocandae; ubi consuetae juxta mensuram non habent. Delphini sunt repandirostrum & incurvicervicum pecus, grande periculum est hypobrychium irrespirabile, aries est animal reciprocicorne, aper Nemorivagus, cerva sylvicultrix: huc faciunt Poetica illa composita nomina cum verbis gero & fero, ad quorum imitationem alia plura confingi possunt; nomina superlativa, patronymica; verba frequentativa, inchoativa, imitativa, desiderativa; omnia denique majoris & seisquipedalis mensurae vocabula.
units.tr: XVII. But when those who have more wit than judgement seek sublimity not only in the sense of a passage but also in the words, what words, what forms of speech do they not bring in? To find metaphors and other tropes they run from one end of the world to the other; things that do not follow of their own accord are dragged in. Periphrases are invented that are enormous and cannot be uttered in one breath. Whatever is great in this universe, the heavens with all their regions and all the stars, all the lands and their peoples, all seas, lakes, rivers, mountains, all the gods and goddesses, in short all monsters, must lend their names, surnames and epithets to the writer, so that by piling these up the grandeur of the style may be increased. The trident is taken from Neptune, the shield of Minerva along with the head of Medusa, the chariot from Phoebus, the winged sandals from Mercury, the club from Hercules itself, and even the three-forked thunderbolt from Jupiter. Xerxes is no longer king of the Persians but Jupiter of the Persians. Vultures are no longer rapacious birds but living tombs. The heliotrope is the Methuselah of flowers. Those who drink mare's milk draw their food from the entrails of the horse. No arrows any longer fly through the air, but feathered deaths claim the sky for themselves. The orator no longer cries out, "What shall I say first, what next?" but rather: What sheaves shall I bring into the barns, and what shall I leave? Here is the formula of a panegyric orator hurrying to the end of his speech: I would wish, I confess, to pass by the new harvests, dimmed by the brightness of the ancients, while describing the deeds you have done in the excess of their greatness as my speech draws to its close. Just as if I wished to count the ornaments of the ethereal axis and, grasping the glitter of the Bears, to describe the beauty of heaven with a powerless tongue, mortal dimness would yield to divine splendour, and the spark of my humble words would not suffice for the torch of the sun. In the end, not even single words please, if they are common; no word has enough dignity, sound or sense. New words must be invented, old ones revived; where the customary ones do not fit the measure. Dolphins are a herd with a hooked snout and a curved neck; a hypobrychium is a great and unbreathable danger; the ram is an animal with a turned-back horn; the boar is a wood-wanderer; the doe a forest-dweller: to this purpose belong those poetic compound words with the verbs gero and fero, in imitation of which many more can be coined; superlatives, patronymics; frequentatives, inceptives, imitatives, desideratives; in short, all words of greater and sesquipedalian measure.

units.la: XVIII. Quum supra diximus, ad sublimitatem orationis facere, si magnum illa & excelsum animum prae se ferat; multi, qui inter veram animi magnitudinem & superbiam distinguere nequeunt, illa dicta sublimia esse existimant, quae sunt arrogantia, superba, ferocia atque impia: quae arguunt contemtum non rerum parvarum, sed rerum contemtore longe majorum atque adeo maximarum, quorum illud animi magni, hoc superbi est. Tale μετέωρον est illud Pharaonis, quis est Jehova, cui dicto audiens sim? tale illud Sennacharibi: quis tandem est ex omnibus terrarum dis, qui suam terram a mea manu defenderit? tale Nabuchodonosoris: Ascendam super altitudinem nubium, similis ero altissimo. Hi nimirum sunt illi μετεωρολόγοι, qui, ut ait Psalmista, de sublimi loquuntur, qui ponunt os suum in coelum, quorum lingua ambulat in terra. Tale est illud, quod Augusto a quibusdam tribuitur, etiam invito Neptuno victoriam se adepturum; Tale illud Caligulae, Jovi suo ita comminantis: Εἰς γαῖαν Δαναῶν περαῷ[?] σε. Hujus adeo omnia dicta, ipsaeque etiam metaphorae truculentam quandam superbiam redoluerunt plane, ut peroraturus, strictürum se lucubrationis sua telum minaretur. Pari arrogantia Domitianus,cum procuratorum suorum nomine formalem dictaret epistolam, sic coepit: Domi-nus & Deus noster sic fieri jubet. Falluntur in hoc sæpe Poëtæ, ut, cum magnum quiddam & sublime dicere volunt, superbum & impium dicant. Sic Lucanus de Nerone Successore eorum, qui per bella civilia multaq; scelera ad imperium pervenerunt: scelera ipsa nefasque hac mercede placent. Idem conserens Cæsaris & Pompeji partes:
units.tr: XVIII. When we said above that sublimity of style arises if the speech shows a great and lofty spirit, many people who cannot tell true greatness of spirit from pride think that the sublime expressions are those that are arrogant, haughty, fierce and impious. These show contempt not for small things but for things far greater, indeed for the greatest, and of these the first belongs to a great spirit, the second to a proud one. Such is the lofty pronouncement of Pharaoh: Who is Jehovah, that I should obey his voice? Such is Sennacherib's: Who among all the gods of the lands has defended his land from my hand? Such is Nebuchadnezzar's: I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High. These, no doubt, are the lofty talkers [μετεωρολόγοι] who, as the Psalmist says, speak loftily, set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walks through the earth. Such is the saying attributed to Augustus, that he would win the victory even against the will of Neptune; such is Caligula's threat to his Jupiter: "I will ferry you across to the land of the Danaans" [Εἰς γαῖαν Δαναῶν περαῷ[?] σε]. Indeed all their sayings, and even their metaphors, plainly reek of a savage kind of pride; so that, about to conclude, one of them threatened to unsheathe the weapon of his own labour. With the same arrogance Domitian, when dictating a formal letter in the name of his procurators, began thus: Our Lord and God orders it done thus. Poets often go wrong in this way: when they wish to say something great and sublime, they say something proud and impious. So Lucan, of Nero, the successor of those who rose to power through civil wars and many crimes: The crimes themselves and impiety please at this price. The same poet, setting out the parts of Caesar and Pompey:

units.la: Victrix caussa Diis placuit,sed victa Catoni.
units.tr: The victorious cause pleased the gods, but the defeated cause pleased Cato.

units.la: Unum Catonem omnibus Diis opponit,si non anteponit. Hercules apud Senecam,si modo Seneca Tragœdiæ auctor est,his verbis à Jove in cœlum recipi postulat:
units.tr: He sets one Cato against all the gods, if not above them. Hercules in Seneca, if indeed Seneca is the author of the tragedy, demands in these words to be taken up into heaven by Jove:

units.la: quid tamen nectis moras?
units.tr: Why then do you weave delays?

units.la: Numquid timemur? numquid impositum sibi Non poterit Atlas ferre cum cœlo Herculem? &c. Da da tuendos Jupiter saltem Deos. Illa licebit fulmen à parte auferas, Ego quam tuebor,sive glacialem polum, Seu me tueri fervidam partem jubes, Hac esse superos parte securos puta.
units.tr: Are we afraid? Will Atlas be unable to bear Hercules, placed upon him along with the heavens? &c. Grant, Jupiter, at least that I may protect the gods. You may take away the thunderbolt from that side; I will protect whichever pole, icy or fiery, you order me to guard. Know that the gods above are safe on this side.

units.la: Typhon aut Enceladus ita loquitur cœlum oppugnaturus, non Heros. Cui non dissimile illud Martialis ad Domitianum epigramma,quo vitam illi longævam precatur:
units.tr: Typhon or Enceladus speaks thus, about to assault heaven; it is not the speech of a hero. Not unlike this is Martial's epigram to Domitian, in which he prays for his long life:

units.la: Esse velis,oro,serus conviva tonantis. At tu si properas, Jupiter, ipse veni.
units.tr: Please, I beg you, be a late guest at the thunderer's table. But if you are in a hurry, Jupiter, come yourself.

units.la: Ita non modo superbus & impius est ille mos Poëtarum, Deos accusandi, invidiam iis conflandi, convitiis onerandi, sed & illæ loquendi formæ nescio quid arrogantiæ & impietatis habent, quibus Dii invidia exonerari, probari, absolvi dicuntur; omnes denique, quæ contemtum sapiunt rerum minime contemnendarum: quales sunt res sacræ, probitas, pietas, justitia, reliquæ virtutes, præstantes viri, dicta factaque præclara, Reges, magistratus, qui nobis præsunt, patria, parentes, jura, leges, patriæ consuetudines, & hujusmodi alia: quæ dicta harum rerum contemtum redolent, nihil veræ granditatis habent. Quod si hæc audacter & intrepide dicta nobis quadam sublimitatis specie abblandiuntur, inde id oritur, quia omnes, quotquot fumus, superba animalia fumus, qui non modo amamus nos efferre supra ea, quae nobis inferiora sunt, qua in re minime peccaremus, sed tum etiam, cum infra vilissimas nos res abjicimus, quasi ad dignitatem recuperandam, nos ipsos supra omne id, quod excellit, evehimus. Quod cum facimus, mirificam voluptatem capimus ex omnibus dictis, quae nos in hac superbia confirmant, haec dicta consideramus tanquam specula, in quibus animi nostri longe grandiores apparent, atque sunt; eaq; propterea tanquam grandia atq; sublimia amamus atque exosculamur. Hanc causam viri perspicaces esse putant, quare omnis orationis sublimitas tantopere audientibus placeat, sapienter certe, si modo inter veram & animi & orationis sublimitatem, & vanum utriusque fastum discrimen agnoscerent. Neque tamen culpandi illi sunt scriptores, qui, cum alios in libris suis loquentes introducunt, superbiam loquentium ipsa oratione depingunt. Egregie T. Livius, cum Servius Tullius rebellem Tarquinium his verbis comprimire vellet: Quid hoc, Tarquini, rei est? qua tu audacia me vivo vocare ausus es Patres? aut in sede confidere mea? hoc Tarquinium & Regi & Socero suo respondisse inquit: Se patris sui tenere sedem, multo, quam servum, potiorem filium regis regni haeredem: satis illum diu per licentiam eludentem insultasse Dominis. Superbus est Tarquinius, qui ita loquitur, at Livius sublimis, qui tantam hujus superbiae in oratione exprimit imaginem. Medeae apud Senecam, cum a nutrice objiceretur, nihil illi e tantis opibus reliquum esse, ad levitatem Jasonis ulciscendam: ita Medea:
units.tr: Thus that manner of the poets is not only proud and impious, when they accuse the gods, stir up hatred against them and load them with reproaches; but also those forms of speech have a certain arrogance and impiety by which the gods are said to be relieved of hatred, approved, acquitted; in short, all those expressions which savour of contempt for things that must by no means be despised: such as sacred things, uprightness, piety, justice, the other virtues, outstanding men, famous deeds and sayings, kings, the magistrates who rule over us, the fatherland, parents, rights, laws, the customs of the fatherland, and other things of this kind. These expressions, which smell of contempt for these things, have nothing of true grandeur. But if such bold and fearless expressions flatter us with a certain appearance of sublimity, this arises because all of us who are men are proud creatures. We love not only to raise ourselves above those things that are beneath us, which would be no sin in itself; but also, even when we cast ourselves down below the most worthless things, we lift ourselves above everything that excels, as if to recover our dignity. When we do this, we take a wonderful pleasure in all the sayings that confirm us in this pride. We regard such sayings as mirrors in which our spirits appear, and indeed are, far greater; and therefore we love and embrace them as grand and sublime. Keen observers think this is the reason why all sublimity of speech pleases hearers so much, and they are wise in this, if only they recognised the distinction between the true sublimity of both spirit and speech and the empty pride of each. Nor are those writers to be blamed who, when they introduce others speaking in their books, portray the pride of the speakers in the speech itself. Titus Livy did this admirably, when Servius Tullius wished to restrain the rebel Tarquin with these words: What is this affair, Tarquin? With what audacity did you dare to call the Fathers together while I am alive? Or to sit confidently in my seat? Tarquin, he says, answered his king and father-in-law that he held the seat of his own father; the son of a king was a better heir to the kingdom than a slave; the slave had long enough mocked his masters through impudent licence. Tarquin, who speaks thus, is proud; but Livy is sublime, who expresses in his speech so true an image of this pride. When Medea, in Seneca, was reminded by her nurse that nothing remained to her of such great wealth, and that she must avenge Jason's fickleness, she replied thus:

units.la: Medea superest: hæc mare & terras vides, Ferrumque & ignes & Deos & fulmina.
units.tr: Medea survives. You see her, who commands the sea and the lands, and the sword and fires and gods and thunderbolts.

units.la: Superba, impia, imo insaniens est Medea, quae ita loquitur; at praeclare Seneca audacis mulieris rabiem his verbis depingit: qua ratione neque Polyphemi meteora in Ovidio sunt reprehendenda; horrida est Polyphemi eloquentia, at Ovidii carmen elegantissimum. In his non id, quod repraesentatur, sed repraesentatio nobis placere debet.
units.tr: Medea, who speaks thus, is proud, impious, indeed raving; yet Seneca depicts the rage of this audacious woman admirably in these words. For the same reason the lofty flights of Polyphemus in Ovid are not to be blamed: the eloquence of Polyphemus is rough, but Ovid's poem is most elegant. In such cases it is not what is represented that should please us, but the representation.

units.la: XIX. Dicendum tandem aliquid est de tertio, partitionis nostræ, meteori genere, ubi duo priora ita concurrunt, ut non modo argumentum orationis sublimis humile fit, sed & vitiosa orationis sublimitas; hoc est infanti non cothurnos Herculis, sed Polyphemi aut Typhonis calceos aptare. Neque tamen defuerunt, neque etiam nunc desunt, qui his meteoris capiuntur; qui se adeo demittere nequeunt, ut res etiam vulgatissimas atque communissimas turgida oratione induant. Aves appellaturi pennatas tibias aut alatos Poetas vocabunt: virginem μένανδρον[?] dicent: Gallum gallinaceum ὀρθροβόον[?]. Quære ex horum aliquo quodnam munus exerceat: Respondebit fortasse ex Sedulio: Ego decachordo psalterio inter beati dogmatis choros Davidica modulationis cantus exerceo. Cantorem in Ecclesia se vult dicere, quære ex alio, ut valeat; Satis bene se in caruncula folliculo constitutum esse, dicet: quid agat, interroga: dicet, se in castris Musarum militare, aut, si scribit, dicet, se aliquid Nihaci papyro gurgitis calamo perarante contradere. Quære, quo anno aliquid factum sit, annum ita describet, post tempora incarnati Verbi, ignea romphea in ostio Paradisi fonte lateris Christi extincta, ut regnum Dei violentius raperetur, hoc vel illo anno res contigit; aut si magnis vocibus magis capitur, quam magnis periphrasibus: dicet, ex nescio quo antiquo tabulario, id accidisse, hoc illove Præsule Archiepiscopante, hoc illove Rege Ptolomante: aut, si cultius loqui velit, dicet, adolescentem in Siciliam venisse tum cum nondum orbis adoraverat Romam, cum nondum Oceanus concesserat Tybri. Parum etiam aberit, quin servo mandaturus, ut ocreas sibi demat, formulâ utatur, quam in hoc casu nescio quis Rhetor magnifice dicturo suadet: Tu qui me inferior es, innutere corporis tui columnis, & ab his mortui bovis exuviis me delibera. Alius familiarem æstatis tempore ex urbe in agrum ad se vocabit his verbis: Iam ver decedit æstati, & per lineas sol altatus extremas in axem Scythicum radio peregrinante porrigitur. Mundus incanduit, glacies Alpina deletur, & hiulcis arentium rimarum flexibus terra perscribitur, squalet glarea in vadis, limus in ripis, pulvis in campis, aqua ipsa quocunque perpetuo labens, tractu cunctante languescit. Etiam non solum calet unda, sed coquitur, & nunc, dum in carbaso sudat unus, alter in bombyce: tu endromidatus exterius, intrinsecus fasceatus, insuper & concava municipii Camerini sede compressus discipulis non æstu minus, quam timore pallentibus, exponere ofcitabundus ordiris:Samia mihi mater fuit. Quin tu mage, si quid salubre tibi cordi, raptim subduceris anhelantibus angustiis civitatis & contubernio nostro aventer insertus, sallis clementissimo recessu inclementiam canicularem. Hunc stylum facile agnoscet vigilax lector, qui Sidonii Apollinaris Arvenorum Episcopi lectitandis epistolis voluptuosam patientiam impendit. Adeo enim ubique sibi constat, ut amicum ne salutare quidem possit, nisi in salutationem erumpat. Ad Papam vero cum scribit, se ipsum superat: Papæ attremit turba collegii: in gravitatis ipsius comparationem ipsa etiam grandævorum corda puerascunt: spiritalia castra eum venerantur tanquam quendam conclamatissimum primipilarem utriusq; sanctorum ordinis: qui manum linguæ porrigit omnibus in conscientia sauciatis, neque proinde est mirandum, quod Papæ se submissurus lixam se & calonem vocat, imo leprosi illius in Evangelio conleprosum. Maxime terribilia meteora Africa produxit. Tale est Martiani Capellæ liber, cujus vel ipse titulus, de nuptiis Philologiæ & Mercurii nescio quid magni promittere videtur. Orditur eum magnificis versibus, quibus Hymenæum invocat; fabulam te legere crederes, quam Romanensem vocant. Omnes Dii Deæque in scenam prodeunt. Singulæ Musæ singula canunt epithalamia. Sponsa tandem deducitur in Iovialem domum, quæ etiam granditate mira mundanum ambitum possideret, & decore conspicuo fulgorem siderum vinceret, & novitate situs signiferum circulum decussaret. Ita loquitur auctor, cum intelligi vult: pleraque longe obscuriora. Legis primum, legis secundum, legis initium tertii libri: per longos & sinuosos Labyrinthi alicujus magnifici sed tenebrosi anfractus putes te duci nescio quo: expectas exitum: subito tandem lux apparet, locum notum agnoscis: In Grammaticam es delatus, literarum, syllabarum, vocum ratio explicatur: hinc quoque ad Dialecticæ prædicabilia deduceris, tandemque; vides heroicam hanc fabulam eò tendere, ut generalia artium liberalium præcepta tradat. Huic terribili meteoro nihilo inferius est Tertulliani liber de Pallio. Auctor notatus erat ab Afris, quod, posita toga, Pallium sumserit: Indignum neque ferendum hoc cum illi videretur convitium; scripsit Apologiam pallii; ubi postquam omnes, quascunque vastissima totumq; mundum complectens imaginatio excogitare poterat, mutationes, ad suam palliandam, adduxisset, & quicquid magnificentissime de pallio dici potest, coacervasset; tandem pallium ipsum loquens introducitur: Adigo, audite pallium loquens, cauterem ambitionis * Dabo catharticum impuritati,* De occursu meo vitia suffundo * De meo vestiuntur & primus informator literarum & primus enodator vocis, & primus numerorum arenarius & Grammaticus, & Rhetor & Sophista & Medicus & Poeta & qui Musicam pulsat, & qui stellarem coniectat & qui volaticam spectat. Omnis liberalitas studiorum quatuor meis angulis continetur. Quisquamne unquam magnificentius, atque hic pallium, verba fecit? Integram ejus orationem adduxissem; nisi stylus hujus pallii paulo esset obscurior; qua virtute vel ipsum Dominum superat. His duobus Afris tertium adjungere possem, Apulejum, in quo multa etiam meteora observabis: modo si papyrum Ægyptiam tu, argutia Nilotici calami inscriptam, non spreveris inspicere. Sed scriptor iste in omnium manibus est, adeoq; a multis amatur, ut, si quis eum reprehenderet, illum invidia nefaria lethali plaga percussum esse clamarent. Nihil audemus dicere, quando Lipsius ipse stylum eius adversus istos de Arpinati Schola invectes pueros, ita eleganter Ciceronis cultores vocat, afferre non verentur. Optandum esset, ut hæc sublimis vid. eloquentia non pueris in scholis instillaretur. Inde enim prima styli corruptio provenit. Eam sublimitatis ideam multi retinent, quam a Præceptore suo acceperant, qui si inepte hic sentit, discipulis eundem tradit errorem. Cum præceptorem identidem audiunt & affectantem & commendantem mellitos nescio quos verborum globulos, dictaque quasi papavere & sesamo sparsa: non magis, ut ait Eumolpus apud Petronium, sapere possunt, quam bene olere qui in cucina habitant: nisi eo sint in pueritia judicio, quod in Henrico Valesio fuisse Frater Hadrianus Valesius commemorat. Digna res quæ hic adducatur: Præceptor Henrici vocabatur Rufellus, homo minime malus, sed admodum imperi-tus & artis, quam profitebatur, rudis & ignarus, qui in prosa eloquentia verba grandia & bene sonantia, orationem in re vel levissima numerosam, plenam pompa & maiestatis, descriptionesque ne in carmine quidem tolerabiles affectabat; qualis est hæc prima lucis descri-ptio, ptio, quam Valesius à ludo recens saepe recitantis more graviter pronunciabat: Dilucescebat: ὡς ἐμῖσα [?] iam uberioris affutura lucis quasi pracone aurora flavescentem auro casariem pullulantibus in altum radius sol matutinus depectebat. Actum erat, inquit Hadrianus, de Valesio, si talem Praeceptorem esse imitatus: sed exemplis magistri malis atque vitiosis judicium discipuli prævaluit. Quam sibi placerent multi Magistri, si tam alte in oratione, ut Rufellus iste, possent ascendere; nunc cum id nō possint, satis sublimes sibi videntur; si discipulis, ut epistolas ita incipiant: Salutem a fonte salutis Amice medullitus peramande: itaque finiant: Tuus per saxa per ignes, &c alias hujusmodi formulas praecipiunt.
units.tr: XIX. It remains to say something about the third kind of meteor in our division, where the first two come together, so that the subject of the speech is not only lifted up in a lofty way but the loftiness itself becomes faulty. This is like fitting the buskins of Hercules to a baby, or the boots of Polyphemus or Typhon. Yet there were, and still are, some who are caught by these meteors. They cannot bring themselves to descend to ordinary matters, but dress even the most common and everyday things in swollen language. Wishing to call birds, they will say "feathered shinbones" or "winged poets." They will call a virgin "a man-abiding one" [μένανδρον]. They will call a cockerel "the early-crier" [ὀρθροβόον]. Ask one of them what office he holds, and he will perhaps answer in Sedulius' words: "I practise the Davidic songs of harmony on the ten-stringed psaltery among the choirs of the blessed doctrine." If he wishes to say that he is a precentor in the Church, ask someone else to do so for him. "I am well enough settled," he will say, "in a little cell," and when you ask what he is doing, he will say he serves as a soldier in the camps of the Muses, or, if he is writing, that he is handing something over to the papyrus of Nihacus, plowing the sea with a reed pen. Ask in what year something happened, and he will describe the year thus: "after the times of the Incarnate Word, the fiery sword, quenched at the gate of Paradise by the fountain of Christ's side, so that the kingdom of God might be seized more violently," and the event happened in this or that year. Or if he is more taken with big words than with big circumlocutions, he will say that it happened, according to some ancient record-keeper I know not whom, under this or that "Archbishop-Presiding" or this or that "Ptolemy-Reigning" King. Or if he wishes to speak more elegantly, he will say that a young man came to Sicily "at a time when the world had not yet worshipped Rome, when the Ocean had not yet yielded to the Tiber." And he will hardly fall short when about to order a servant to take off his boots, using the formula which some rhetorician, I know not who, suggests for a speaker who wants to sound magnificent in this case: "You who are lower than me, lean on the pillars of your body and free me from these dead ox-hides." Another, calling a friend from the city to his farm in summer, will do so in these words: "Now spring is passing into summer, and the sun, raised along the furthest lines, stretches its beam into the Scythian axis, travelling abroad. The world has grown hot, the Alpine ice is destroyed, and the earth is written over in the winding of gaping cracks; the gravel grows foul in the shallows, the mud on the banks, the dust in the fields, and the water itself, flowing ever onward wherever it goes, languishes in its lingering course." Nor does the water merely grow warm; it is boiled, and now, while one man sweats in linen and another in silk, you, wrapped in a hunting-boot outside and bound up inside, pressed into the hollow seat of the Camerine municipality, yawning, begin to set forth to your pupils, pale not less from the heat than from fear: "My mother was from Samos. Nay, rather, if you have any care for your health, be quickly drawn away from the gasping narrowness of the city, and eagerly joined to our company, and by the most gentle retreat of the shade escape the canicular harshness." A watchful reader will easily recognise this style, one who has spent a patient pleasure in reading the letters of Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of the Arverni. For he is so consistent everywhere that he cannot even greet a friend without breaking out into a salutation. When he writes to the Pope, he surpasses himself: "The crowd of the college trembles at the Pope: in comparison with his gravity even the hearts of the aged grow childish; the spiritual camps venerate him as a most renowned chief centurion of both orders of the saints; he who stretches out a hand of speech to all wounded in conscience." Nor is it any wonder that, when about to submit to the Pope, he calls himself "a camp-follower and sutler," or even, in the words of the leper in the Gospel, "fellow-leper." Africa produced the most terribly grand meteors. Such is the book of Martianus Capella, whose very title, On the Marriage of Philology and Mercury, seems to promise something great. He opens it with magnificent verses in which he invokes Hymenaeus; you would think you were reading a fable of the kind they call Roman. All the gods and goddesses come on stage. Each Muse sings a separate wedding-song. At last the bride is led into the Jovial house, which by its marvellous size would possess the mundane circuit, and by its conspicuous beauty would outshine the brilliance of the stars, and by the novelty of its position would cut across the zodiacal circle. So the author speaks when he wishes to be unintelligible, and most things are far more obscure. You read the first book, then the second, then the beginning of the third; you are led, as through the long and winding passages of some magnificent but gloomy labyrinth, you know not where. You wait for the way out; suddenly at last a light appears, and you recognise a familiar place. You are carried into Grammar, where the theory of letters, syllables and words is explained; from there too you are led to the predicables of Dialectic, and at last you see that this heroic fable tends toward delivering the general precepts of the liberal arts. Nothing less terrible a meteor is Tertullian's book On the Pallium. The author had been reproached by the Africans because, having put aside the toga, he had taken up the pallium. Thinking this insult unworthy and intolerable, he wrote An Apology for the Pallium; in it, after he had brought together every change that the vastest imagination, embracing the whole world, could devise for the sake of cloaking his pallium, and had heaped up everything that can be said most magnificently about the pallium, at last the pallium itself is introduced, speaking: "I drive out," hear the pallium speaking, "the cautery of ambition. I give a purgative to impurity. I pour out vices in my encounter. They are clothed in my garment," and "the first teacher of letters," and "the first explainer of the voice," and "the first sand-tracer of numbers," and "the Grammarian," and "the Rhetorician," and "the Sophist," and "the Physician," and "the Poet," and "he who plays on music," and "he who conjectures the stars," and "he who gazes at the winged things." "All the liberal breadth of the four studies is contained in my corners." Did anyone ever speak more magnificently than this pallium? I would have quoted his whole speech, but the style of this pallium is a little too obscure; by this virtue it surpasses even the Lord himself. To these two Africans I could add a third, Apuleius, in whom you will also observe many meteors: "provided you do not disdain to inspect the Egyptian papyrus, inscribed with the subtlety of the Nilotic reed." But this writer is in everyone's hands, and is so loved by many that, if anyone found fault with him, they would cry out that he had been struck by a deadly blow of nefarious envy. We dare say nothing, since Lipsius himself does not hesitate to bring forward his style, calling those who inveigh against the boys of the Arpinate school, so elegantly, the worshippers of Cicero. It would be desirable that this lofty, I mean, this eloquence should not be instilled into boys in schools. For from there comes the first corruption of style. Many retain that idea of sublimity which they had received from their teacher; and if he thinks foolishly here, he hands the same error on to his pupils. When they hear their teacher again and again both affecting and commending I know not what "honeyed little balls of words, and sayings sprinkled as with poppy and sesame," they cannot be any wiser than, as Eumolpus says in Petronius, "those who live in the kitchen can smell well," unless they have that judgment in boyhood which Brother Hadrian Valesius records in Henry Valesius. The matter is worth citing here: "The teacher of Henry was called Rufellus, a man by no means bad, but very unskilled and ignorant of the art he professed, who in prose eloquence affected large and sonorous words, a rhythmical style even in the slightest matter, full of pomp and majesty, and descriptions not even tolerable in verse; such is this first description of light," which Valesius, in the manner of one who often recites what he has recently learnt at school, pronounced gravely: "It was growing light: as [ὡς ἐμῖσα] the dawn, already about to give more abundant light, like a herald with its golden hair, the morning sun combed out the yellowing locks with its rays sprouting upward." "It was all over with Valesius," says Hadrian, "if he had imitated such a teacher; but the judgment of the pupil prevailed over the bad and faulty examples of the master." How pleased with themselves many masters would be if they could rise as high in their speech as that Rufellus; now, since they cannot, they seem lofty enough to themselves. And if they teach their pupils to begin their letters thus, "Greetings from the fountain of salvation, dearest friend, loved from the marrow," and so to end them, "Yours through rocks, through fires," and similar formulas of this kind.

units.la: X X+ Sed &c extra scholas in vulgaribus linguis meteora inveniuntur. Pleni sunt illis Itali, pleni Hispani scriptores; Germani multi eos in his imitantur. Galli hodierni saniores patribus atq; avis, veram tandem, fulgoribus his relictis, scribendi formam animo sunt complexi, quam si retinere possent, est autem difficile huic genti diu aliquid retinere, proxime eorum eloquentia ad priscam illam, quae in Graecia Demosthenis & Romae Ciceronis tempore viguit, accederet. Supersunt tamen in omnibus linguis hodiernis, nescio quae meteora priscis incognita. Haec sunt formulae illae, quibus alii aliis observantiam & reverentiam testamur, complementa vocant, ad quod significandum neque Graeci neque Romani ullum nomen invenerunt, verba honoris quidam appellant; ubi magnis & nescio quid promittentibus verbis nihil fere significamus; dicere se humilimum atque obedientissimum alicujus servum aut mancipium, nihilo plus significat quam Graecorum χαῖρε & ave Latinorum: ut alias longiores atque sublimiores formulas taceam. Nemini suaderem ut haec, ubi illa consuetudo poscit, omitteret: optandum tamen esset, ut paulatim politiores homines hanc ineptam consuetudinem dediscere possent; non tot inutilibus vocibus oratio inflaretur atque enerva-retur.
units.tr: Outside the schools too, however, figures of speech are found in the vernacular tongues. Italian and Spanish writers are full of them; many German writers imitate them in these things. Modern Frenchmen, wiser than their fathers and grandfathers, have at last embraced, having abandoned these glitters, the true form of writing; if they could keep it, for it is difficult for this people to keep anything for long, their eloquence would come closest to that ancient eloquence which flourished in Greece in the time of Demosthenes and in Rome in the time of Cicero. Nevertheless, in all modern languages there remain certain figures of speech unknown to the ancients. These are those formulas by which we bear witness to one another of esteem and respect, which some call complimentary expressions, though neither the Greeks nor the Romans found any name for signifying this, and which some call words of honour; where, with great and somehow promising words, we signify almost nothing: to say that one is the most humble and most obedient servant or slave of someone means no more than the Greek χαῖρε [chaire] or the Latin ave. I say nothing of other longer and more lofty formulas. I would not advise anyone to omit these where that custom demands them; yet it would be desirable that by degrees more refined people might be able to unlearn this silly custom, so that speech would not be puffed up and enervated by so many useless words.
